utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We're very grateful to everyone for accommodating the change to the sitting schedule at short notice, and can now confirm that this week we will sit from 9.00 to 3.30 each day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning again, Mr. Delic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We will continue with examination-in-chief from Mr. Cepic in a moment. Please bear in mind the effect of the solemn declaration continues throughout your evidence. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. But before I start I owe one document which is related to the incident from 14th of the April, 1999, and bomb attacking on column of civilians. That is the exhibit 5D1158, and actually this is the combat report from 52nd Artillery Brigade from the Djakovica. That report is described bomb attack on column of civilians between Djakovica and Prizren.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: We stopped when we were discussing places of worship. I would like to continue now. In the places where members of your units were, were the places of worship preserved?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Places of worship were preserved, you knew that the headquarters of my brigade was at Prizren, and while my unit was in Prizren all the places of worship were fully preserved. Among them is the most important Muslim religious building, Sinan Pasha's mosque and another 30 mosques in Prizren. There's also the Catholic church, several Orthodox churches, and monasteries.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. While we're waiting for the technical conditions for the video clip to be played to be made ready, I will ask you something else. What was the ethnic composition of your units and the units that were resubordinated to you?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the professional soldiers are concerned, the ethnic composition was mixed. The officers were of all the ethnic backgrounds from all the communities that lived in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and as for the units the ethnic composition was also mixed. But in the reserve force all the ethnic groups living in Kosovo and Metohija were represented, Turks, Muslims, Goranis, Albanians, and naturally Serbs and Montenegrins, a small number of Macedonians, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Were there entire detachments made up of people of Muslim faith?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The 68 Military Territorial Detachment was composed of Goranis, they're Muslims, and there was also a unit from Recani, it had a Muslim majority. There was another unit where Turks were in the majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, regarding the military territorial detachments, can inhabited areas also be part of the defence system in accordance with the military doctrine?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In accordance with the military doctrine, yes. But in our particular situation, given the total air supremacy of the enemy and given that the ground aggression had not started yet, the inhabited areas were not part of the defence system yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Is that the reason why military territorial detachments were moved out of the inhabited areas?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was one of the reasons, to prevent the concentration of troops in the inhabited areas, in towns and villages, which would make those inhabited areas targets for air-strikes on the one hand; and on the other hand the relocation of the military territorial detachments ensured greater security for the territory where there were inhabited areas, towns and villages, because they guarded certain territories and roads around those inhabited areas. And in my zone they also guarded the border itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. We will go back shortly to the town of Prizren. Can you please tell me, during the war what was the situation like in the town of Prizren. Did people move out of that town?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was some small-scale moving out of people from Prizren, but people moved into Prizren too, especially from the surrounding villages so that Prizren -- well, I can't tell you now specifically because nobody did any censuses during the war, nobody was counting the population, but it may have had more inhabitants than in peacetime. I concluded this on the basis of a report I received from some of my officers whose families faced a problem: They couldn't buy bread. And then I inquired about the quantity of bread being baked in the town of Prizren, and they told me that the wartime capacity was about 30 per cent larger than in peacetime.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we see now 1242,5D; actually, 5D1242, document related to Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, do you recognise this footage?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, because at that time I was in Prizren. This is the 13th of June. I was there until the 14th of June. I left Prizren on the 14th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Let us just look at one brief excerpt from this footage.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This mosque that you can see here in the background, that is Sinan Pasha's mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, we've seen white-and-blue vehicles in this column of vehicles, we saw some civilian vehicles. What was this all about? Do you know? What were those vehicles?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know because I watched this column as it left. These are the Serb civilians leaving and the police units leaving, the police and their families.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, are these two separate video clips that we have seen?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: No, this is one video just to speed up procedure I cut it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You see, one of them had a date -- the first one had a date along the bottom, and then this one has the letters "N & N" at the top. Are they actually the same video?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: We received this video as one video clip, but probably it is made from separate views or sources -- separate sources. There is the same title on all -- during all clip "N & N."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And we can clarify with the witness if it's necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, last week we had two other video clips that also have this exhibit number. This exhibit number, I think, has actually 30 separate video clips, some of them completely unrelated, and I have a concern about how we're going to handle that because there's nothing to distinguish the video clip from Exhibit P1242 [sic] we played last week, and the second one we played last week and this one today. We need to have some way to identify them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is your office the source of these?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Cepic, I think there may be a question of authentication of these and clarification. I'm not suggesting that's a fundamental problem; it's, I think, a technical problem that you have to resolve so that we can disentangle one from the other. These essentially show two separate things. One showed very jubilant celebrations and the other shows, you say, Serb civilians and police leaving.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: With your leave, Your Honour, I can clarify with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I showed you those clips during the proofing and you've just seen them now in court. Could you please explain to us. We've seen the markings in the upper left-hand corner "N and N." Could you explain what this is.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This marking in the upper left-hand corner, it is the name of a photo shop in Prizren. It was close to the army hall. The person who recorded this is a Muslim, and I know that I received the whole cassette in 2001, but it was for my personal use. At that time I knew the name of this man. He owns this photo shop and he used to do some work for the army. He would record some of the activities we had, and on this occasion he filmed everything that happened in Prizren when KFOR troops arrived, it's a German brigade, and at the same time the Serb civilians and the police, the military, were leaving. So these were two simultaneous actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we just -- can you just play a short part of the first section, Mr. Cepic?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. It has the "N & N," but there was a part of it where the date showed, the 13th of June appeared on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: The next part of video is marked with the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You can stop there then. Mr. Delic -- yes, this part, this is done by the same person, is it? It has the initials at the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: He didn't hear the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry. Mr. Delic, is that by -- is this part produced by the same photographer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. This is a tape that's more than two hours long, and you can see my troops here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cepic, these --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They -- on this cassette you can see the arrival of the German soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That takes care of this immediate clip, but I still have the problem about Exhibit 5D1242. On Thursday we watched a segment about a bombing or a bomb in Nogavac, that also has this exhibit number, and I don't know how we're going to distinguish these clips.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just hold on a second. Mr. Delic has just mentioned two hours of filming. Is that two hours 5D1242 or is 5D142 -- 1242 the two hours plus other things?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. We have one video exhibit which is almost more than one hour, and the content of that video is related, as my learned friend mentioned, Nogavac and some other places. We just have couple minutes related to Prizren on this exhibit, 5D1242.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So what you have is a small extract from the two hours that Mr. Delic mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, okay. Well, it looks as though you ought to at some stage produce a filing which identifies the make-up of 5D1242 so that there is no doubt that -- about the areas of the film or clip which relate to different episodes along the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May I continue with your leave?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we see the third part of the film. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, do you recognise this monument?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the monument to Czar Dusan because otherwise Prizren was called a Czar city because the Serb Czar Dusan for a time had his capital city there and because the Archangel Gabriel with Czar Dusan's church is to be found in the vicinity of Prizren and it is from the stones of that church that Sinan Pasha's mosque was actually built.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Cepic, the filing will have to specify the footage so that we can relate it to the evidence. At the moment it would be very difficult to relate what you've played to the questions that have been asked, but you can do that later by reference back to the transcript. Whoever has compiled the video clip should be able to do that for you. Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, we'll move on to another area. We heard testimony in this courtroom that after the beginning of the NATO bombing, in the vicinity of Prizren, there was shooting at the army, at the troops, and that your soldiers then from the rear battalion found a local Albanian who was interrogated and executed. Was something like that possible?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time that I'm hearing of anything like that, and something like that is just not possible. I know that in the town of Prizren itself - and we're already talking about the month of May - that right next to my logistics unit an Albanian was captured and he owned up to being a member of the KLA, and he also told us where he had left his rifle and showed us his rifle and all his other equipment; but later on he was handed over to the military police authority, and he was sent up for a court-martial.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do we have a name or any way of identifying this person?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have exhibit related to that matter, and I think that during the break we will tender it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, we heard testimony to the effect that there was an order that the police and army were taking ID cards at the border crossings and setting fire to them in order to prevent the Albanians being able to claim that they originated from Kosovo. Did such an order ever exist?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such an order did not exist and no normal person could have issued an order like that, because everybody has their documents with their personal identification numbers, there are records of various sorts. And as far as the army is concerned, it was never at the border crossings at all because the border crossings were guarded by the border police and that's where the customs office is. The army seized the rest of the border. However, as I say, nobody could have issued an order like that, nor have I ever heard of any such order being issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: We'll deal with something related to orders and authorisation, but, General, tell me something, General, without permission from the superior command, can you arrange actions with MUP?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Without permission from the superior command, no activities, either independent activities or activities in conjunction with MUP, would be possible. For any such action, you would have to have permission from the superior command. And we've had occasion, and I've said this earlier on in my testimony, that there was several situations like that where I asked permission from the superior command, and pursuant to their request I sent out my concept for carrying out an action and then I would receive the okay from my commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, the command of your brigade or the subordinate units, did they combine any combat papers or maps on decisions for MUP action?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw no need for that. At the level of the brigade, I compiled documents for my own brigade, I drafted them, and those documents are well-known. My subordinate units would, for example, take battalions. They would see to the lesser documents but they would compile documents and maps just for themselves. I don't want to enumerate all the things necessary for the different levels, the different documents for the different levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you exercise control of the MUP units? Did you check their work, control them in any way?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was just not possible because everybody is in charge of his own units. I controlled all my subordinate units, but the MUP units were not subordinate to us. So I had no authority as far as they were concerned, and ultimately it wouldn't have been proper to do so. It wouldn't have been proper for the army to control the MUP, and the same would be true vice versa, it would be quite out of place. And all this has to be regulated first and foremost by some orders for activities like that to take place, so that kind of thing never happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did the MUP units send you reports?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The MUP units have their own chain of reporting towards their own officers and commanders, just as I do. I have my chain of reporting toward -- up the chain to my superiors. It is true, but this was more to help out my colleagues. I knew when the MUP units had suffered losses and when they were faced with a difficult situation, and especially in town. We would learn when some of the MUP units were killed, just as people knew when a soldier was killed and especially when a commander was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have on our screens P2077, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, is this an order of yours?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is an order from my brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Would you explain point 1 to us. You don't have to read it out. We can all see it and read it, but explain it to us, please.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Among other things, in this order it says that a large number of soldiers and officers were doing their job in the best possible way, but that a lesser number were violating regulations, and that is why this order was issued, which forbids military personnel to stop civilians or civilian vehicles, that they forbid them to steal, carry out ID checks. And then it is underlined that ID checks are allowed only in the combat operations area, which is quite normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What was the object of an order of this kind?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, once again, officers were cautioned and told that everyone within their area of defence should take care of the behaviour of every soldier and every officer under his command, and that one and all were requested to work lawfully. And the military police company that is mentioned here and in the title, in the heading, as well, it is being issued the assignment of organizing patrols and to take into custody all violating of this order and regulations that hold true in the army generally and that the perpetrators should be taken to court.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we take it that prior to this document being issued there were examples of each of the categories listed, that's 1, 2, and 3, that you were aware of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already said that there were individual cases. I said that in my earlier testimony, especially with soldiers along the roads, because the entire communication line, the roads that civilians passed by in order to cross the Vrbnica border crossing and enter Albania, goes through the defence zone. And so some soldiers were standing along the roads to prevent civilians and people from going into the minefields. And in one of the documents we looked at earlier on, we were able to see how many soldiers violated those regulations; and this order, roughly speaking, and the report was roughly at the beginning of April, which means there were individual cases where money was taken away from civilians and vehicles were taken away from civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Theft, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could we have on our screens 5D892, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, what does this document represent?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a criminal report which the military police of my brigade raised against a soldier, and the subject is: "Theft under Article 165 of the Criminal Code of the FRY," and then we have an explanation as well of what the soldier did, the act he committed. There were a number of such criminal reports. This is probably just one such example. For every case, for every offence that we learnt of, either in the unit, through the military police, or whether it was reported by civilians or by the police, all those cases were investigated and criminal reports filed with the war courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we see 5D893, please. I'm sorry, Your Honour, we have one error in transcript, page 14, line 9, I think that witness said "war courts," not law courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, this seems to be similar. Would you explain briefly what it is.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a criminal report once again filed by the -- from my military company, the authorised person, but -- and under the same article against a different soldier. And it is the same day, the 16th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we see P962, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, is this document familiar to you, the one we have on our screens?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could you explain it to us, what it's about.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a list of filed criminal reports against perpetrators of criminal acts in the zone of my brigade from May 1998 to July 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we see the number 44 in this list, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, can you look at number 44, please.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: It says Zeljko Jokic?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this case?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am. This was the only case of rape that took place in my brigade, although my police company did arrest some other persons for rape from another unit. But as far as my unit is concerned from the 2nd Motorised Brigade from Djakovica, in fact, this was the only one, and the rape was committed in Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Will you just explain briefly how you detected the identity of the said person.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He committed the rape in end April during the night. The next day those civilians called the police, the police carried out an on-site investigation, took witness statements, invited the military police because it was said the person who committed the rape was wearing a military uniform, but there was no other information except that the other soldier who was protecting him had used the nickname Brzi to refer to him. Then we sent a telegram to all units asking everyone to check whether they had a soldier nicknamed Brzi in their unit, but we expected to find that someone in a unit in Prizren and it took us more than ten days to find out that there is a soldier by that nickname in the 2nd Motorised Battalion in Djakovica. Then we took him into custody and brought him before a war court.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we see Exhibit P2010, in B/C/S page 17, in English page 34.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I have already shown you this document during proofing.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have the right-hand side, please, in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you explain in the upper part of the page we see 20th May 1999. In English there is a mistake, unfortunately, it's not the 10th of May, it's the 20th of May.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a telegram sent from the command of the 2nd Battalion to the command of the 2nd Motorised Company of that battalion, requesting that urgent information be submitted about volunteer soldier nicknamed Brzi. It says he's probably on the border post Liken. After identifying the said soldier, bring him back to the 2nd Motorised Company where the organs of the military police would arrive.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have Exhibit 5D1367, please. 1367. In B/C/S, page 24, in English page 32, please. In B/C/S we need lower corner of left side, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, please look at the bottom left corner and explain.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the 2nd Motorised Company of the 2nd Battalion informs on the same day the commander of his battalion that Zeljko Jokic, nicknamed Brzi, speedy, indicating birth date, is in his unit and will be brought to the command of the company on the 21st of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we see Exhibit Number 5D1367, please -- I'm sorry, 1351, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, is this your document?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a report sent to all the units of my brigade concerning some criminal offences, criminal actions, and negative currencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Look at the third paragraph, please.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a description of the incident we discussed. There's a description of the whole epilogue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, was anyone else arrested besides Jokic for the same incident?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His helper was also arrested. He was found in the same battalion and arrested, plus some other soldiers who were not from my unit were also arrested for the same criminal offence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Is the co-perpetrator Zlatko [as interpreted] Krsmanovic from the 2nd Battalion?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for the reference, the name of that soldier is also in the Exhibit 5D1367, in B/C/S page 33, English page 43, co-perpetrator for -- in this -- in that incident, described incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And in transcript is a small error, page 17, line 17, Vlatko Krsmanovic, not Zlatko. Could we see 5D889, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, in the upper left corner do we see an indication to your company of the military police?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is another criminal report from the military police company of my brigade dated 17 April. This is precisely what I referred to. Three soldiers, one of whom committed the rape while the others are accessories. They are from the 52nd Brigade of the anti-aircraft defence in Djakovica, whereas my military police company was covering the territory of Metohija, so that the civilian police who first found out about the incident reported it to the military police. The perpetrators were found, the injured parties were found, and this entire procedure followed -- was followed from a medical examination of the injured parties, taking witness statements. And these three soldiers were immediately arrested and turned over to the wartime court. I reported about this to the corps commander, and I also -- in fact, the commander of the 52nd Brigade whose soldiers these persons were also reported it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we see again P962.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, in this overview I counted last night around 65 names of persons against whom criminal reports were filed for the criminal act of ordinary and aggravated theft, and nine persons were charged for seizing motor vehicles. Did you also include criminal reports for the most serious crimes?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These include criminal reports for all criminal offences committed in my brigade or in the area of responsibility of my MP company that I learned about in any way whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we see the number 60, 6-0.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Look at number 60, Slavoljub Topalovic.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Will you explain briefly.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a soldier, private, from the military police company who killed a civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Was he immediately arrested and handed over to the authorities?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure if he was arrested on the same day of the perpetration or the next day, but he was immediately turned over to the wartime court.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Number 84, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, do you see number 84, Vujadin Stekovic?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Tell us, first of all, what rank he held.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain first class.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What was he responsible for?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In one combat action when he ran into a terrorist ambush, after another unit lent them assistance, he found three civilians in the vicinity. He ran into three civilians and killed them. He was arrested the next day, and he was taken before a wartime court.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we see numbers 103, 104, 105, and 106, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you see these names, Mancic, Tesic, Seregi, Radojevic, what are these cases about?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have a major, Mancic; privates Tesic and Seregi and captain Radojevic. Similarly, in a combat action against the terrorist group they killed two civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Were charges filed against them?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not find out about this immediately. We learned about it after the war was already over so that criminal reports were filed after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we see number 131, please, same exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, while we're waiting, is it the case that even on the most difficult circumstances in terms of movement you did send your suspects to appear before a wartime court?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We would take and keep perpetrators in custody in the unit for no longer than one day, and that's according to regulation, and after that we would escort them to Pristina to appear before a wartime court.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Would you look at number 131, something about kidnapping.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the 11th of April. Five persons were kidnapped, Captain Tanaskovic was the leader. He was a member of the reserve force of the military police. He was a leader of this group, and he was escorting two persons to wartime court. He was accompanied by Dragoljub Cvetkovic and their driver was Dragan Vucetic. The persons who were under arrest were Zarko Filipovic and Zivota Todorovic. They had been arrested for theft. They were kidnapped between Prizren and Pristina on the road, more precisely in the area of Suva Reka.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did you have any further information about them?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were killed and decapitated. Their heads were torn off and there was reporting about that in Serbia as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is two soldiers killed by their colleagues?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I'm not understanding it, sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two out of these five soldiers had perpetrated a criminal offence; the others were taking them to the wartime court. The captain was the leader of the group, there was also the driver, and another person as an escort, and they were killed by terrorists, terrorists who kidnapped them in the vicinity of Suva Reka. They stopped their van and took them towards Budakovo, and we found the van at a later stage -- actually, it was in May. And finally we learned about the fate of those soldiers because the terrorists took photos of themselves with those soldiers whose heads had been severed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have two photos related to that matter, but actually those photos are not permitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us just clarify one thing. How many of those were killed, all five of them or just two?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All five of the soldiers, and there was another case when just one soldier was kidnapped. So a total of six soldiers were kidnapped. The fate of the five is known, they were killed, but as for the sixth, his fate remains unknown to this day. He was also being taken to the wartime court.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. My last question: In the period while General Lazarevic was your superior officer, did you ever receive any orders that would be aimed against the civilians or any orders that would ask that you commit a criminal offence, either in writing or orally?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never received any such orders. General Lazarevic always insisted on lawful conduct and he insisted in particular on the protection of civilians. The Rules of Service envisage that an officer cannot issue such an order and the Rules of Service also bind any person who receives such an order not to carry it out. At any rate, soldiers and officers alike are not allowed to commit any criminal offences and they do not face any sanctions if they refuse to obey such an order. In fact, they must not obey such an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General. This was my last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cepic. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I will be dealing with paragraphs 24 and 48 of the indictment, that is the favourite topic of my colleague, the Joint Command. This will be very brief, and let us achieve some results. When Mr. Cepic asked you, you showed the envelope in which you received the orders from the Pristina Corps. From time to time there would be the orders from the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija in that envelope, and you said that after the mission was completed a combat report would be sent to the Pristina Corps command, because you thought that this had been a task issued to you by the Pristina Corps. My question to you is: Where did you hand in this combat report, to whom and where?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, combat reports, as usual, would be handed in my command, the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Where was the headquarters of the Pristina Corps command during the war?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the war, when we're talking about combat reports, they're not handed in directly, they're -- they are sent in an encrypted form to the Pristina Corps command using communications equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell me, just a brief question. In addition to you, the Pristina Corps and MUP, did the air force and air defence have their officers in the Pristina Corps and perhaps even in your brigade?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is envisaged by the Rules. During the war I had an air force liaison officer, and at the corps command there was a group of those officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: They were part of what chain of command?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In addition to being in touch with me, they were also in touch with their own command.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So despite the fact that they were also part of the Army of Yugoslavia, they represented the forces of the Army of Yugoslavia, but their chain of command was separate from yours?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And if I had any requests vis-a-vis them, they had to talk to their command to get an approval.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can I then conclude that in the operations during the war you had three independent commands: Your own command, the MUP command, and the third one, the air force and air defence; is that so?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, at that level.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Fine. Now I would like to ask you the following: You've seen those orders from the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija. A general question for you: They have a specific role in the indictment which is not quite clear to me, but it will become clear to me once I see the judgement. In this text, in those three or four pages, were any orders issued that would have anything to do with ethnic cleansing, for instance, an order for you to kill, rape, burn mosques, conduct ethnic cleansing, anything that would be in contrary with the Rules? Is there anything of the sort in there?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite the contrary. They are professionally drafted orders, and it appears that the only problem is the heading.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Fine. So if we were to replace this heading with the one that is contained in normal orders, so instead of it saying "Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija," we have, for instance, the Pristina Corps command, and then the same text. Is there anything dishonourable, anything unlawful in those orders?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is a proper, professional military order, there are no omissions, no deficiencies in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: My second question: If you look at the text in its entirety, does it deal specifically with the orders issued to the army, to the elements of the Pristina Corps, telling them what to do?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exclusively.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Are any orders issued to the MUP or to the air force and air defence in this order?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Orders are issued only to the subordinate units of the Pristina Corps, to us, giving us tasks in a specific action.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now look at something in those orders, the orders that pertain to your unit, there are seven, eight, five, six, whatever, I will not be showing all of them to you, that's not important. But I would like you to look on your screen at P2015, that's one of them. I selected this one at random, believe me. And while we're waiting for this to show up, can I ask you: Where was the headquarters of the Pristina Corps in peacetime and in wartime?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In peacetime the HQ was in the Pristina Corps command building, it's in the centre of Pristina. And during the war, the command post moved about every few days.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: We heard testimony from Colonel Filipovic, who said that the command post of the Pristina Corps never moved back to the four-storey building during the war. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do agree with that. My commanders are not amateurs, they're professionals. They will not -- they would not allow themselves to make such a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In all those orders of the Joint Command, there are 15 or 16 of them and a couple of them refer to you, or rather, six or seven refer to you. Could we please look at item 11, that's on the last page in Serbian and probably in your language, or rather, in English. Item 11, and could we please zoom in. General, as you can see, in paragraph 48, General, it is stated that command was exercised through Joint Command, and these papers serve to corroborate that, they are evidence of that. No, I'm referring to 24 and 48 of the indictment. In item 11 it says: "Command and communications." According to the indictment, the corps, MUP, and the air force and the air defence, all the forces, were under the command of the Joint Command, and could you please read the first line in item 11.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Command post of the Pristina Corps in the building of its peacetime location" --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And what does it say afterwards?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The communications with the Pristina Corps command and the subordinate units is to be maintained in accordance with the existing communications document with obligatory use of the general encryption documents."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. General, I heard what you said, all of us heard what you have said about all those papers so far. Is it possible -- so we're not talking about whether it's true or not, because we can either place our trust in you or in what the Prosecutor says, we have the indictment on one hand and what over a hundred witnesses said on the other. Is it possible that things operated in this way, during the war, in a wartime, as it is described here?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is impossible --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, I think we need to note that this document is dated the 23rd of March, before the war started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Not only that, at the moment the question is incomprehensible to me, and it sounds like an argument rather than a question. If you could reformulate this question, if there is a serious question in there rather than a submission, then let's have it clearly formulated so that we can understand clearly the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in item 11, in the lines that we've just read, it is indicated how command would be exercised had this been an order exercising command.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: My question is: Is it possible in wartime conditions to exercise command in this manner from this post?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is impossible. As I've already said, that would you be a total disaster to be in a peacetime location and to exercise command from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So that was my question: Was there anyone there in the peacetime location?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the Pristina Corps building was empty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How does this -- a moment ago you said that all of these orders were written in a very professional way. How does that fit with this reference here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my opinion, this actually fits in because probably whoever was drafting this order, that was the operations organ of the corps, had in mind that if this order or any parts of this order were to fall into the hands of any person who is not supposed to have it, that then that person would get a wrong -- would get wrong information about the location of the command because there was danger that the command might be bombed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The Prosecutor objected, saying that this was a document dated the 23rd of March, the day -- that was on the eve of the air-strikes. When was this order actually carried out?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was carried out on the 25th, a day after the air-strikes began.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So much for the Prosecutor's objection. So among other things --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I move to strike that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, that should have come from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: It's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us move on to item 13 of the same document. It says here -- could you please read the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija shall command and control all forces during combat operations from the Pristina sector."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Fine. So first of all we can conclude that "all forces," refers to the MUP, to air force and air defence, and to the Pristina Corps. Now, this Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija involved civilians, the Prosecution alleges, three or four at the beginning, but at any rate --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters couldn't hear the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: While you received any orders or -- did you notice any civilians exercising command over you, MUP, or air force and air defence?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, naturally I didn't notice anything of the sort. I was in the field with my unit, but in all combat operations that I carried out I would be in touch with my commander from time to time, General Lazarevic. I would report to him in certain situations, and he was the only person that I was talking to because he was my commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was the forward command post of the 3rd Army there at the command post of the Pristina Corps, where General Lazarevic was?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. General Pavkovic was at the forward command post of the 3rd Army. I know that because General Lazarevic and General Pavkovic would visit my unit, the former more often than the latter.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you ever see Nikola Sainovic during combat operations anywhere in any function, and in particular exercising command over Pavkovic, Lazarevic, you, air force, MUP, or whoever?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw Mr. Sainovic in any combat operations. I think I saw him on one occasion in Pristina when I received a decoration.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That would be all.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There are two matters you would perhaps clarify for me, Mr. Delic. You made it clear that you had an air force liaison officer in your command. Are you also saying that you had MUP officers or a MUP liaison officer in your command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I didn't think so, but it was the impression of pushing them all together that changed my earlier understanding. The second question is -- that I need clarification on is this: What does that last sentence in the order mean, "the Joint Command for Kosovo from the Pristina section shall command and control all forces during combat operations"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I'm concerned, Mr. President, it doesn't mean anything to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So -- but let me stop you there. How does that fit in with this idea of a professionally written order that you were dealing with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already said how I, a commander, at lower levels and other brigade commanders, how we understood the term "the Joint Command" in the first place. We understood it, or rather, we felt that "Joint Command" needed to be written because of the coordination between the MUP and the army. Had it said on this order "the Pristina Corps" in the heading and had it been signed by the command of the Pristina Corps, had it said that, then the order would have been quite all right; but it would have been quite all right as far as I'm concerned as the commander from the army. It would not have been acceptable for the command of the MUP detachment, for instance, because, quite simply, he did not want his units and he personally to be commanded by the army because until resubordination this is an order that was issued before the order on resubordination was issued. Now, had the situation been the reverse, had it said in the heading that the MUP issued this order and had MUP signed it, then it would not be acceptable to me because I did not want and it was impossible in actual fact pursuant to our rules and regulations for me to be commanded by somebody from the MUP. So this is some intermediate solution and when it says in the heading the Joint Command, then the same order is sent to the MUP and sent to me in the army. So then it is acceptable for me too and for the man in the MUP and then we can coordinate in the field because he knows that he has to report back to his command, that is to say the MUP command; and I know I have to report back to my command, which is the command of the Pristina Corps. So that is the only way in which I can explain this and interpret it. Coordination and joint activities in any other way could not be decided upon in the field. There might -- there could have been perhaps some other term used instead of "Joint Command," but something as I say that would have been acceptable to one and all, that is to say to the MUP units and to the army units, because they are units which belong to different state institutions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic -- sorry, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Can we clarify something because quite obviously your first question came out of a question that I did not put clearly enough. You asked him whether he had a liaison officer from MUP, and he said he did not. But I asked him about the time when there was joint activity with MUP officers, if you remember, and he said the day before yesterday that the two commanders were together.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But that was not a liaison officer. I was there and the commander was there in the same place, so that he did not send me his representative nor did I send him my representative. He was in command of his own troops and I was in command of my troops. We were in the same location, nearby, for us to be able to organize the joint activities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think we all now understand each other. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, let's go back for a moment to the period prior to the beginning of the war and war conflict. Can you tell me, on the basis of the knowledge you have about the events that took place in your area of responsibility and linked to the KLA forces, something more precise about what weapons the KLA had in the first half of 1999 until the beginning of the war? And to help you out, we've already had a witness and I'm going to tell you something that he told us they had, that the KLA had. So if you have anything to add or any comments to make, I would invite them. First of all, let's take artillery weapons -- infantry weapons, rifles, AK-47, Kalashnikovs, semi-automatic rifles --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there an issue over this, Mr. Hannis, how well-armed the KLA were?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Not really, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's the real problem with this? Is this -- are you trying to get information we don't already have or ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I'm trying to get information from the witness that we have not heard thus far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, very well, if it's new information --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in order to shorten the procedure, I'm already giving him a list of what the other witness said so as not to waste time and have this witness tell us the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: As we were saying, rifles, AK-47s, Kalashnikovs, semi-automatic rifles, light machine-guns, heavy machine-guns, that is as far as infantry weapons are concerned. General, among the ranks of the KLA, to your knowledge, was there anything else that they had, any other infantry weapons?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. Of the infantry weapons what was left out was the snipers. Terrorist forces had the most up-to-date sniper weapons. Of the sniper rifles manufactured in Yugoslavia, they had the M-76, 7.9-millimetres, then the sniper rifles, Soviet produced of the 7.62 calibre, then they had sniper rifles of a western manufacture, but state-of-the-art, the most sophisticated in the world, I quote the SIG Sauer one and then there were large numbers of those. Then there was the sniper rifles of the 12.7-millimetre type of Yugoslavia manufacture there was the Crna Strela, black arrow, then US-manufactured ones, and I'd like to stress the American military rifle Barrett of the 12.7-millimetre calibre because the terrorists had large numbers of those as well. And let me just mention the Kalashnikovs were manufactured mostly by China, but there were also Albanian-manufactured ones pursuant to a licence and there were a certain number of Kalashnikovs which were manufactured in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Just a short question linked to this. What was the range of the sniper rifles, especially these special, sophisticated ones you've just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The special rifles had a 2-kilometre range.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, my next group of questions also relates to weapons, anti-tank weapons, a 500-metre range Zoljas, mortars, the recoilless guns, recoilless cannons, grenade guns, and anti-tank mines -- grenade launchers and anti-tank mines. That's what the witness -- the other witness told us. May we have your comments, please.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the hand-held launchers manufactured in China, they're called the 150 type and 500 type, that is to say their ranges are 150 metres and 500 metres. Then we had our own hand-held hand -- rifles, 600 metres. And in addition to the Zolja there were the Osas of the 90-millimetre calibre also produced in Yugoslavia. Then there were the Russian type hand rocket-launchers -- hand-held rocket-launchers as well as the German ones, sophisticated ones in any case, anti-aircraft and anti-armour weapons. I can't remember their names just now, Armbrust, yes. Now, in my area we seized a number of these weapons Armbrust which were packed as they had been sent out from the factory and far more numerous than our army had. As far as the mortars are concerned the 60-millimetres ones were the most frequent and in my zone alone, we seized about 40 such launchers [as interpreted]. And then we had the 82-millimetre launchers [as interpreted] and 120-millimetre ones as well. Now, as far as the recoilless guns are concerned, the characteristics of those guns are the following: They were manufactured according to an American licence, 76-millimetre calibre, but they were not only intended to hit armoured targets where the range was up to 800 metres, they could also be used as artillery support, because they had special fugue grenades, and a particular device which allowed them to have a range of up to 7.100 metres, these high explosives. So that, generally speaking, is what the terrorists were usually equipped with, but after the war broke out they also used heavy artillery and tanks from the territory of the Republic of Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, with your leave, just one error in transcript. I think that page 35, seventh line, witness mentioned mortars, not launchers, also in 8 line, not launchers, but mortars.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you mean to distinguish launchers from mortars, Mr. Delic?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour, but I think that witness could clarify for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I've asked the witness, not ...

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you mean in this to distinguish launchers from mortars?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Because the -- I find the whole answer quite confusing since it's not been done in a -- you haven't been asked the questions briefly enough to give us clear answers to it, but -- these questions just asking the witness to comment on a whole series of things you say, Mr. Visnjic, don't help to make the job of final adjudication here easy, and this is just an example of the sort of confusion that can arise when you ask the witness just to comment in general. He's being asked to comment on evidence we have already as well, so one wonders what the value of that is. Please continue, though, as quickly as you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can give you a partial answer to your question. On pages 5879 and 5980, that's the reference, that's the testimony of the previous witness. And what the General confirmed, or rather, added here was precisely what's going to be our reference, and that is the range, what the range was of the weapons that the KLA had in its possession. So I think that will be important later on during our further analysis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just to give you an example. The first ones that were referred to which were Chinese with numbers 150 and 500, which related to the range, I don't know what these weapons are in light of his answer. I don't know if they're mortars or rocket-launchers or Zoljas or what they are, but we just have an amalgam of material that we're going to have to go away and work with and try to make sense of.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes, I'll check the interpretation later on. What I heard from the witness was clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, these weapons, or rather, let me put it this way: The KLA organization in your area of responsibility -- well, I have a separate question linked to the role of the village staffs. Now, can you tell me to the best of your knowledge whether the village staffs were included in the KLA; and if so, in what way?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1998 there was a KLA organization, so it was just from mid-1998 that the operative units of the brigade appeared, but the village staffs remained. The situation was similar in 1999, the brigades existed but there were also village staff -- guards or village staffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, the village staffs, were they a component part establishment-wise of the KLA units or were they separated from them with separate commands?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had the same command, but they were the territorial component, whereas the brigades were the operations component which moved from one territory to another. The village watches or village staffs stood in defence of their own village.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, General, at the beginning of 1999, how would you describe the activities of the KLA with respect to planning actions and the training of terrorists, if we compare it to the previous period in 1998?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in 1999 there was a noticeably better type of organization and the terrorists were noticeably better trained as well, and in planning their actions too they were better -- although in 1998 and 1999 the actions had a terrorist character right up to the beginning of the war. There were ambushes and that was the most frequent way in which the terrorist forces acted against the MUP forces and against the forces of the army as well as rapid attacks, surprise attacks on MUP check-points along the roads. So sudden attack inflicting casualties and then a speedy withdrawal from the location.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, during this period --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I just have a question for clarification. I'm sorry, General, to bother you with this. Now, what were the areas in which these people were getting training, particularly in 1999, I mean the KLA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The KLA trained on the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, but also throughout 1998 and 1999 in Albania. Massive training took place in Albania. I can name some centres Tropolja, Sahan, Vucedol, Kukes and a string of other places. I'm talking only about the period of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: If the training grounds in Kosovo were accessible to you and your intelligence, why was there a lapse on the part of the intelligence and the Pristina Corps not to nip it in the bud then? Why did you not make efforts or what were the reasons for not making efforts, allowing this training to continue right under your nose if it was at all taking place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those places were not accessible to us, and that is especially true of the territory of Drenica, Mount Milanovac and the Drenica area, especially in 1998. Now, as a soldier I cannot tell you why measures had not been taken in 1998 to stop that activity in a drastic way. In the beginning, we as soldiers we reported about it. Some of my reports from 1998 were mentioned here with exact references to training locations and the number of terrorists there, but I suppose that even the superior command to me could not take these steps. It had to be ordered from a much higher level, and our country at the time was under great political and diplomatic pressure and I believe that could be the reason why it had not taken that step, being under embargo to nip these activities in the bud. It was expected through political measures, through negotiations with Albanian leaders outside of the extremist KLA wing an agreement would be reached to resolve this in a peaceful way, and that is why the mediation of the international community was accepted. All the time in 1998 there was a wish to resolve the crisis in Kosovo and Metohija peacefully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: We also find that you've given us names of various brands of weapons with which the KLA or the other people whom you called as terrorists were equipped. I mean, it seems they had all the brands from the world, and here too we find an inaptitude or a lack of efficiency on part of the Pristina Corps or those involved with security to check that coming in. And now you also tell us that geographically that area may have been inaccessible but there the training was taking place. No area is inaccessible geographically, and you had all the sources to control it at the relevant time and particularly before the embargo. So I was wondering if there can be any explanation to that, but being a soldier who -- you have to tell us, and you were quite in charge of things, who else is going to tell us, in case you can, sir. Thanks a lot.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. Let me just tell you one thing about the embargo. It lasted for about ten years continuously in our country throughout the crisis in the former Yugoslavia, and we were under political pressure all the time. I don't know the name of one of the documents that Mr. Cepic read during the previous day of my testimony, but from that document you can see that I as commander reported to General Pavkovic at the time where the terrorists were in my zone, where they train, and how many they were. And I asked for an order to be issued to my unit to execute certain military drills from that territory, to be present constantly on the roads, and to prevent the expansion of terrorists from that area. But even General Pavkovic could not order me that; he had to seek approval at a higher level. As an army, we had our hands tied to a great extent in terms of the measures we were able to take against the areas we knew as terrorist locations. It would have been much easier for me, it would have been really easy for me to do that. I wouldn't even have needed the support of another unit. That area within my zone included a location where there were no more than 200 terrorists. If I had received that order at the time, the terrorism wouldn't have spread from my zone; but it was the political framework that decided at the time what the army could or couldn't do. If we had done it, we would have been subjected politically and diplomatically to even more pressure, threats, and condemnation, because it was already being said that we were violating the human rights of Albanians. Now, as for the state border across which arm smuggling took place, we had the right to deal with that. My border units and my own units engaged in a large number of clashes and skirmishes on the border, trying to stop it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: And then my -- another question, sir, I'm sorry to bother you with another question. Then we -- I would be very anxious, if possible -- if possibly you could tell us, then what was your mandate there? I mean, there were restrictions doing this, restrictions doing that. I'm not talking about the humanitarian aspect because that is something we are all supposed to observe, but what was your mandate then? And if you can answer now or after the break, whatever. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. Of course I can answer. There were only a few things we could do, one, to conduct combat training within our unit; to protect our military installations, second; and three, to protect the state border. During 1998 we received another assignment, to defend roads, and no more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Now, when you talk of protecting roads and protecting borders, that is a defensive duty of course. But then weren't you given the mandate to fight people whom you thought were militants?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We could only respond if our unit was attacked, and after July 1998 when the terrorists attacked and captured, took control, of a town numbering 30.000 people, that's the town of Orahovac, then at state level a decision was made to engage in a five-stage plan. It was only then that we received orders to develop plans for certain areas holding terrorists, to neutralise them, disarm them, rout them, to kill those who refused to surrender their weapons, but that was only in the end of July 1998. By that time the terrorists held about 90 per cent of the territory of Kosovo and Metohija and most of the roads.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We will have our break now and resume at 11.20. Mr. Delic, could you again leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, let us go back to the KLA. Did you have first-hand experience with the assistance given to the KLA by the official authorities of the Republic of Albania before or during the combat activities?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. The very fact that on the territory of the Republic of Albania, even close to Tirana itself, but especially in places close to the border terrorists were able to train in 1998 and 1999 speaks volumes. All this was done with the knowledge of the Albanian state, the Albanian government, the Albanian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, did your troops have direct fire contact with the units of the Albanian army in the course of 1999?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in 1999, sometime in the middle of May, on the route going across Kunara mountain, a tank company attempted to launch an attack on our border, that was one incident; and during the Strela 2 operation from the 26th of May approximately until the 8th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How did KLA forces communicate between themselves on your territory, what kind of communications equipment did they use?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For their own internal communication they used radio devices, small-powered radio devices, up to 5 watts, similar to those we used. They had communications similar to ours, but they also used one kind of telephone, especially in 1998. It's the kind of telephone where the receiver is portable and has a range of several kilometres where the base is kept in a house. That was typical for Kosovo and Metohija, and of course they had hand-held radios, Motorolas, Midland, Jessica [phoen], and other types.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know how they communicated with units outside your zone with their commands abroad?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In addition to ordinary communications, they had satellite phones. On one occasion in December from a group that was crossing over from Albania, it was between the 14th and the 15th of December, we seized two satellite phones, complete with laptops and encoding equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: At that time it was state-of-the-art communications equipment, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was state-of-the-art because between our units we did not have that type of communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now pull up Exhibit P2447 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: This is a map of Kosovo marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we zoom in the lower half where the letters A and B can be seen. Once again, please. Could we zoom in once again. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, this map shows a large part of your area of responsibility. One of the Prosecution witnesses drew on it in orange the territory held by the KLA, including the defence positions. Before I put my question, could you draw in the roads that were off limits to the Serb army and police in the second half of 1998 and 1999, roads that Serb forces couldn't use except escorted by the UNPROFOR. I believe you've said something about this, but since it's technically possible to do electronically could you draw that. I'm talking about the period before the war, and when I said "UNPROFOR," I meant KVM, the Kosovo Verification Mission.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The road that was completely off limits to us is the road from Djakovica across Mrasor and could be used to go further on to Srbica or fork off to Pristina. Then another road from Orahovac via Malisevo, also to Pristina. The road from Orahovac to Suva Reka was completely cut off, closed. The road from Suva Reka to Stimlje was also critical.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you draw it in a dotted line, please, then.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because convoys had to be accompanied, escorted, and maybe I should show some other roads that are outside my zone, such as the road from Decani to Pristina. The road from Malisevo to Banja was completely cut off, as was the road from Malisevo to this road that in turn leads to Pristina. The other roads here, these roads here, were sometimes under threat, and in this area here from Djakovica to Prizren one had to be extra careful.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Can we stop here. Let me just explain that markings made in bright red and in a solid line designate the roads that were completely cut off and off limits, and bright red dotted line indicates the roads that were -- that were critical. Did I understand you correctly, General?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And my colleague has just alerted me to the fact, what was the situation with this road to Prizren, this little part there?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a dotted line. One could travel there during the day but not during the night; during the night it was prohibited.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. General, could you just --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can you give the General the other colour of the pencil, blue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I think that you can actually see that, but could you tell us, based on your knowledge, what territory was held by the KLA in your zone before the war started. And let me just tell you that the Prosecution witness drew in -- marked the territory that was held by the KLA in his opinion, and these markings are made in orange. Do you have any corrections to make?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a correction should be made here. Celina should also be a part of it and then it would be fine, and here we should include the whole part just Malisevo.
