So this entire territory should also be inside this area to link up with this line that was drawn by this witness, and then if we were to leave my zone then some other areas should also be included. But as far as the rest of my zone is concerned, I think that this was done quite properly with the amendments that I just made.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just stress for the record that the witness marked in blue two semicircles, indicating the territory that should be added to the area marked in orange, designating the area held by the KLA in the critical period during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, in the zones marked as A and B on this map, which KLA brigades were deployed there to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In area A where it says "Reti," that would be Retimlje. That is where the command of the 124th Brigade was, and in this area where it says "Samodreza," that's where 122nd Brigade was located to my knowledge. That's as far as the A and B areas are concerned. Further up to Malisevo in the Dragobilje-Marali-Janciste areas, in Dragobilje there was the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that's where the 121st Brigade was located. In Budakovo there was the 123rd Brigade, that is according to what I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And Budakovo, for the record, is in the area marked B on this map, that's on the right-hand side of this drawing. General, were there any KLA units in Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the town itself, the town of Orahovac in 1999, there were none. But in the villages south of the village of Brestovac, there were terrorist forces and to the west the village of Potocani, Gratotine [phoen], Drenovac, Zatric, Poluza, Poznik, that's where they were. So Orahovac was in some kind of an encirclement, although it was possible to move in and out with a certain risk from Orahovac to Prizren and Djakovica. As for Malisevo, it was impossible to go in that direction. In March already it was impossible to go there, in February only police patrols went there escorted by the OSCE.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, could you tell me what was the situation like in Suva Reka. Were there any KLA units in the town itself?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And how far were the closest units from the town itself?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the village right next to Suva Reka, it's now covered by the red line so you can't see it, but it's the village of Rastane it's on the outskirts of Suva Reka in the direction of Orahovac. That's where the first check-point was set up there at the bridge, check-point of the terrorist forces. So it was impossible to go any further down that road.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I apologise. How far is that bridge from the centre of Suva Reka?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think it is 1 or 2 kilometres away from the centre of Suva Reka.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It's continue on the other side.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the other side the village of Recani, Bukos, and this whole territory that is encircled by this colour, by the markings made by the previous witness. And then on the other side in the direction of Prizren, the villages of Djinovci, Lesane, Spinadija, Lutoglava, Ljubizda, they were free. There were no terrorists there, but there were terrorists in Grejkovce, as close as in Grejkovce and Selo Gradiste. In Musitiste there were none. In Delovce there were none, that's because there was a mixed population there, half Serbs, half Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, when you say that the KLA was in a village, that doesn't mean that there was a KLA presence. But as far as I was able to understand from earlier testimony that means that there were some fortified areas there, fortified positions held by the KLA; am I right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That means that such a village could not be entered without fighting, you had to fight your way in.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you launched this action on the 25th of March, 1999, let us not now go into detail because you've already explained all that in your examination-in-chief. What knowledge did you gain about the movements of the civilian population within the areas or zones covered that included the KLA positions?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this zone marked A, I was close to Orahovac. I was in -- on the high ground about 300 metres above this area here. I personally was able to observe columns moving down the roads that had been constructed in 1998, and they were moving to Neprebiste, Mamusa, and further on to Studencane, Doberdolan, and Pagarusa. Those columns could be seen on the 26th and the 27th. On the 25th, according to the reports that I received from my commanders, in this area here, the area of Nogavac there was a small group of about 200 civilians who were instructed to go back to their village of Nogavac after the army had passed through it and I think to Celina. And according to a report from the commander of combat Group 1, some of the population from the Pirane area went from Pirane and from Ram Dubrava towards Medvece and Ramus, that's in area A. When I went to area B later on the road leading from Orahovac through Ostrozub to Malisevo, I personally saw columns being formed in the villages of Janciste, Kravoserija and Moralija; but the columns that were formed in the village of Janciste and Moralija were heading in my direction towards Ostrozub and the columns from Pagarusa and Kravoserija were heading towards Belanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, when you say that you saw the columns being set up if I understand you correctly and heading in various directions, am I right if I say that at the time when those columns were being formed, in order to move out there were no combat activities in the territory of their villages?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In fact, when I observed these areas from a distance of about 2 kilometres, this is what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The way I understand you, some of the population moved towards you, towards the army, and the other one was moving in the opposite direction, away from the army, moving in the direction opposite to the movement of your forces. How do you explain that?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not give it much thought at the time because the important thing was for the people moving in my direction to be able to pass through safely and not to be fired on in any way. But now that I think about it, when these people appeared on the main road they were supposed to slow down the advance of my unit because I and my equipment, we were using this road to move forward, and they were also supposed to slow down the MUP unit because, after all, they had to check, they had to verify, whether there were any terrorists among those people moving in our direction because we had had such instances in the past. So I have no other explanation apart from that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. General, were there any movements of the population in the villages of Retimlje and Studencane before the start of the conflict in March 1999?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: To your knowledge was that organized by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the people from Retimlje were moved as early as in February because the KLA was in Retimlje, this entire brigade, with its command, its hospital, and the population was in Opterusa, Studencane, Samodreza, those areas. On several occasions when my columns were moving from Prizren to Orahovac and from Orahovac to Velika Hoca, they attempted to go to Velika Hoca, it was immediately observable that the villages of Opterusa, Studencane would get organized, that civilians would gather there, and that tractor columns would be set up, and that they would get ready to move in the opposite direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. For the transcript, General, on page 50, line 6, the villages mentioned there should be Retimlje, Opterusa, and Studencane.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Just a few more questions. General, you were a brigade commander and later on you were promoted to higher posts in the military and your last post was the head of the operations -- chief of the operations administration in the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, if I'm not mistaken. In light of the posts that you held and the experience that you have from exercising command at lower levels to processing information at the highest level, I would like to ask you the following: The kind of action that was carried out in the period from the 25th of March until the 24th of April that you described in your examination-in-chief -- I apologise, not the 24th but the 4th, the 4th of April. So this kind of action, as far as I understand it, in the sense of military technology covered in a number of reports heading: To the higher levels of command. In your opinion, bearing in mind the number of levels involved below the level of the General Staff, what kind of information would reach the General Staff that might be relevant for this level of decision-making at the General Staff? So what kind of information would be needed at General Staff level for the decision-making there? To be more specific, we saw your report about one of your actions there. It has a couple of pages. Then we have a corps report that contains even less information, and then we have the army report that contains even less information. So in light of this -- if we bear in mind this operation in Malisevo, what kind of information would actually reach the General Staff that would be relevant for the decision-making?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you in a position to answer that question from your own personal knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I was the acting chief of the operations administration that brings together all the information at the General Staff level for the General Staff and for the state leadership; that is why I am in a position to answer this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, what was that, Mr. Delic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was from 2002 until the end of 2004.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So your answer is based on your experience then, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Based on my experience after the war, when I was serving in the operations administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How is that going to help us, Mr. Visnjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it would help us to get the witness's opinion on that, and I have -- I have the exhibit containing the analysis of this information that I can proffer later. So maybe in light of those two things, the opinion of the witness about what kind of information would be needed at the General Staff and what was actually contained in the report, perhaps it could give us some idea about what kind of information is expected at the General Staff level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We're agreed that we would not be assisted by knowing Mr. Delic's opinion based on what happened when he was acting chief of the operations administration. What we want to know is what actually happened during the war. So please move to something else, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, just interrupt for a second. Are you telling us now that inferences are not possible? Then all the inferences that the Prosecutor is trying to draw from 1998 cannot be applicable in 1999. I ask kindly for the clarification of this matter, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This particular issue is what we're addressing, and Mr. Delic's experience was between 2002 and 2004 when -- now, we're not -- it's not part of the -- it's not part of the job of this trial explore what the circumstances were like in 2002 and 2004, and only then could we see what happened then had any bearing on what was actually happening in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have to establish first whether the rules of procedure changed at all or not, and if it's established that it has never changed then we can draw references.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let's have the Rules of Procedure; if they haven't changed them -- if we look at them, we don't need to look at 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's -- please let Mr. Visnjic to clarify with the witness whether these rules have changed or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've made our decision. Please move on, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no further questions for this witness, and perhaps it was a misunderstanding. What I wanted to have through this witness is in relation to the chain of information -- the flow of information, how much information would reach the top. There was no intention to use this to prove what was necessary in this particular case, in 1999, or rather, what was actually needed -- necessary, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, we've already heard evidence from virtually every senior general in the Supreme Command Staff, all of whom could have told us specifically - and indeed in some instances have told us specifically - what the information available was. So it -- we do not understand how on earth what a man who was not involved in the General Staff at that time could tell us based on his experience in 2002 and 2004 that would not require us to explore in detail differences in the circumstances in these two distinct periods of time. You've had every opportunity to deal with this through witnesses who were there at the time. I should also say to you that we've now had fairly significant, what has been effectively evidence in chief, from both Mr. Fila and you from a witness who is not listed as one of your witnesses. If this is going to be a regular feature of the presentation of the Defence case we will have to review the order in relation to the distribution of the remainder of the time because there's probably been a significant chunk of time taken today in what effectively adds to the examination-in-chief that we've provided for Mr. Cepic. Now, that will make the presentation of the Defence case exceptionally long beyond what is proportionate to the Prosecution case. So if that is a practice that's going to be followed, we will insist now in having notification in advance to the extent to which you envisage examining in chief witnesses for other parties, giving notice of what that examination-in-chief will be so that we can consider it, and then we would have to review the allocation of time so that it accurately reflects the proper distribution of the 240 hours for the presentation of the Defence case. So please consider that carefully, bearing in mind all the evidence we've had already on these areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know how you were able to reach this conclusion on the basis of my cross-examination because this is the only witness that I examined -- cross-examined for more than 20 minutes, so I really can't see how you were able to reach this conclusion on the basis of this witness, that I went beyond the scope of -- beyond what was allotted to the Prosecution. This was the only witness that I questioned for more than 20 minutes. This has not been my practice so far. Of course it is up to you to reach conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm only indicating to you, Mr. Visnjic, so that there can be no misunderstandings later that extensive examination-in-chief by other counsel of another accused's witness does tip the balance, and I entirely accept that so far that has not been your practice. And therefore, there's no need at this point in time to take any decision based on what's happened today. I'm simply observing that these are circumstances of which we have to take account of, bearing in mind the opportunities that you've had earlier to raise, for example, the particular question that's given rise to this controversy. The -- I also anticipate, although Mr. Cepic will no doubt correct me if I'm wrong, that Mr. Delic is one of the most important witnesses that will be led by the Lazarevic Defence and possibly the one that will be here the longest, and therefore he is exceptional in that sense and not the basis on which we would make any specific order. There would be to be a practice developing before it would be appropriate for us to review the position further. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We will give an IC number to this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC152, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My name is Branko Lukic, and I represent the Defence of General Lukic before this Tribunal. I am going to ask you some questions that will try to throw more light on certain issues, principally with relation to the police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have on e-court to start off with Exhibit 5D1351, please, and my colleague used it earlier on today during his examination. May we zoom in, please, the first part of paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, in line 7 it says here - and you explained this case - you said that you had prosecuted this soldier and his name is Zeljko Jokic - and in line 7 it says: "Jokic Zeljko went from flat to flat introducing himself as a policeman or as the police and throwing out all the residents from their flats." Now, this one of the reasons that slowed down his detection, because first of all you didn't know whether he was a policemen or a soldier?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If you look at the criminal report filed, we did know that he was a soldier because he wore a military uniform; however, since he didn't give anyone his name, all we knew was his nickname, which was Brzi, or speedy, and we thought he was from some unit located in Prizren, whereas he was from the 2nd Motorised Battalion, which was otherwise in Djakovica in peacetime, and was in the 2nd Company as well, which provided security for the -- of the defence area facing the Likane border crossing to Radanovici border hut. So that's what slowed it down.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have P1995 on e-court next, please. And may we have the last page, or rather, let's have the first page first and then we'll go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you see what the document is? You discussed it today. Are the letters too small for you?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think we discussed it today but last time, during the last sitting. And could we zoom in a bit, please? Yes, I can see it now and I do know the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now let's look at the last page of this document in the B/C/S and English. In the first paragraph, the second sentence reads as follows: "The command of the forces was by the combined command of the MUP and the Army of Yugoslavia." You explained to us today that at the command post there was someone from the MUP and someone from your command, usually you and the commander of the detachment --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- I think we may have to go back one page in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question to you, General, is this: In this document, this combined command of MUP and the Yugoslav Army was mentioned as you described it, right --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, Joint Command, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We looked at this the previous day, and, yes, I did say that in most of my documents where it says that there was a combined command and that I as brigade commander or commander of the military unit and the command of the MUP detachment, that we were at the same place because in this way it was easiest to coordinate action in the fighting. And as to this specific case, the one you're asking me about, in the region of Suva Reka there was the MUP detachment commander with my deputy, and I was in the Orahovac area with the deputy commander of the MUP detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In order to clarify this situation, is it true and correct that in that location there were no civilians or no politicians?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was combat, that would be risky business and absolutely not permitted. There was only the MUP commander with a few of his men, and I myself from the army with a few of my men which were there for that command post, the security detail, the driver, and that was it. So that was the same on the MUP side.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now on e-court may we have Exhibit 6D677. May we zoom in to the left part of the map. We're interested in the 549th Motorised Brigade -- [In English] Move back two steps. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, looking at this map, can you explain by telling us and also by drawing on to the map in red, using a red pen, what the area of responsibility of your brigade was. Could you tell us and draw it in.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The area has already been drawn in.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, but for the Trial Chamber to gain a better understanding.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that you also mentioned that a difference exists between the area of responsibility in peacetime and in wartime. Now, can you explain using this map what the difference is?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There is a difference between areas of responsibility in peacetime and in wartime. In peacetime the area is far broader, the surface area is much larger.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So what area is this, the one that you've drawn in, is that a peacetime or a wartime area?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a wartime area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also said that during the war, during the state of war, from the Pristina Corps you received an excerpt from a map defining the zone or area of defence of your brigade. Now, can you use a blue ink to indicate the area of defence using this map.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the width is concerned, it is the same as you can see here, and here you can see that -- you can see my troop deployment here. So I can just draw in where my units were to emphasise that. This is the plan of defence showing the different stages. You wanted me to use a blue pen, so I'm going to highlight my units, where my units were deployed, that is to say the 2nd Motorised Battalion. This is one of the companies of that battalion, this one here, the 1st Motorised Battalion; the 3rd Motorised Battalion; the 108th Detachment in the later period. And you can't see it here, but towards the Macedonian border, that's where the 68th Detachment was and that is where the 354th Detachment was. Here you can see that this was my artillery, in fact. And here, once again, right close to the town is the anti-armoured artillery battalion, and that would be it as far as my forces go, as far as I can see. So those would be the areas of deployment of the units. There are some other small details here, but I can't read it on the map. The map is just a basis. I use it to compile my own map for the plan of defence and battle.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We see that the area of defence has been defined by four points, and you can see the breadth and the length of the area; am I right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the depth. Now, what is the defence area or region and how is that determined?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The defence regions are determined by lower tactical units, platoons, companies, and battalions, and they are determined by using three points. Two points, as you can see here, in front and one in-depth. And the sector of the platoon company or battalion is the immediate sector which is taken up by this unit and in which lower units have their defence positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the -- that all these defence sectors taken together of these lower units and all the units together make up the area of defence of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The area and gaps in between and the distribution of command posts and the distribution of logistics units all together make up that area, the area of defence. And of course in that area you also have other units, if I can use the term.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you asked a question there: "We see that the area of defence has been defined by four points and you can see the breadth and length of the area." What are the four points?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that we cannot see other two points on this map, Your Honour, but there are -- actually, we can see probably two and two are close to the Albanian border.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But what are you meaning by points? We've got six areas that were drawn on the map by Mr. Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If we can ask the witness to clarify this. I'm not willing to testify. I'm not an expert, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's the trouble. You see, you were testifying because you simply say: "We see the area of defence has been defined by four points," and he says: "Yes." And I assume you would know what the four points were and I was hoping you would tell me and make it easy.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think my question was whether the zone of responsibility is defined by four points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But I can clarify with the witness in the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, is it true and correct - I apologise, but we have to go back to this - the area of responsibility of the brigade, is it defined by four points?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the area of responsibility is defined by many more points, but the area of defence is defined by these -- the four points.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My mistake. You're quite right. Yes, the area of defence is defined by four points. Now, defence, is that a type of combat activity?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Defence is a form of combat activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we then agree that the area of defence of a brigade is also the area of combat activity?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, with the proviso that in the area of defence of a brigade you can also have other units present outside the organic composition of the brigade as defined by the order from the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that you organized and put into effect the regime on the ground and the civilian population in taking care of the population, how they moved around, the exit and entry regime, and you all coordinated that with the civilian authorities, such as MUP and other civilian authorities, and in keeping with Article 193 of the rules governing the brigade?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we're dealing with the border belt - and it is a belt that was 5 kilometres to begin with and later on 10 - then I have authority over the area contacting and regulating the security regime, especially in the areas in blue here in the border belt, when it comes to the gaps too, the spaces in between. But if you look at the entire area and as concerns the entire area, everything linked to the civilian population in that area was done by the local self government and they coordinated their efforts with me. When it came to the road going from Prizren to Vrbnica which the civilian population used to leave our territory. There was certainly coordination there principally with the MUP because the MUP held control of the Vrbnica border crossing. The customs and border police would check people leaving, but since that whole road until the place of Zur had been mined, there had to be coordination with my own unit because I first had to demine part of the road at the border itself and then later on with my men to ensure that there were no -- to provide security and ensure that there were no casualties if anybody entered a minefield because -- and of course daily communication existed with the chief of the secretariat with respect to the problems that existed in the area itself. And if anything untoward were to happen or if the civilian population were intersected, if there was any theft or seizing of vehicles and that this was noticed by the MUP members, by the MUP force, that was certainly reported to my military police company, and the check-points of the army that were located along the roads coming in and going out of town - or in certain situations they would be reported to me personally for me to be able to take measures and steps. Now, in a similar way we would inform the MUP if we were to notice anything untoward happening on the territory which did not come under our competence and something that the MUP should see to and resolve; or if there was something linked to the members of the police force generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And not only the police force but the civilians too?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Because the MUP was in charge of civilians too. Thank you. Now, I have just one more question from this group of questions related to areas. Is it true that the brigade command organized and implemented security in the area of combat activities, or rather, the area of defence coordinating its actions with other subjects in defence pursuant to Article 227 of the brigade's rules?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the border belt itself the army deals with these issues on its own outside the border belt, however, it coordinates with the authorities for whom this is their main job, their main purview. However, the army has full authority over its own members in the border belt, but as far as the civilian population is concerned it had to be coordinated with the authorities, the local self government, but primarily with the secretariat of the interior in Prizren, Djakovica, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to ask you about terrorism in 1998. You have already told us about terrorist attacks in 1998 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just hold on. I'm not sure the English can be right on this last answer. In the border belt -- Mr. Delic you said: In the border belt the army deals with security on its own and outside the border belt however it coordinates with the authorities for whom this is their main job. You then went on to say, according to the English: "The army has full authority over its own members in the border belt, but as far as the civilian population is concerned it had to be coordinated with the authorities, the local self government, and primarily with the secretariat of the interior in Prizren, Djakovica, and so on." Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you give us the answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I was trying to say was that the army always, regardless of whether it's a border belt or any other area in its zone, has full responsibility for any measures it takes towards its own members. In the border belt it has responsibility for controlling others as well, primarily the civilian population; outside the border belt it coordinates, when civilians are concerned, with the local self government and other state authorities, but primarily the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. That makes much more sense. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm not following English translation, so I'm sorry that I missed this one. Before we move on, I kindly ask for this map on the screen to get IC number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Before we leave the subject, Mr. Delic, and before it disappears from the screen, what are the four points defining the area of defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the north there was one point on the state border; in the west -- to the west of border post Mitar Vojinovic, that's this brook here, I can't read the name, that's the first point. The second point, I think it's the village of Crmljanje possibly here. In the south we cannot see that on the map unless we can move the map, it's a peak on Mount Sara, Peskovi peak, 2.551 altitude, so there are two points to the south-west and two points to the south-east.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, again it may be a problem with English translation, but there's only three points mentioned in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, since we are all interested apparently in these four points, could you take a pen, a green pen preferably, to mark the points you see on this map and use numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, if you can see all the four points; if not, just tell us where they are.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the south-east cannot be seen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please make this as simple as possible. I don't know whether it's important or not. It's only because Mr. Lukic has raised the matter. There's no point in raising it and then not understanding it. There are two points in the north and two in the south; is that the position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but in the south we cannot see the point. The map is -- we don't see that section of the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But can you mark the two in the north on the map as you see it at the moment? Just mark them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I marked them with number 1 and 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you gave us a name for one of the ones in the south, that was a peak on Mount Sara called Peskovi peak; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what was the other one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's Prevalac, it's a pass on the road from Prizren.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's enough for me. Thank you. Mr. Lukic, we'll give you a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC153, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, we said we would be talking about terrorism in 1998. To what extent this terrorism had an effect on the confidence people had in state authorities, do you know that from personal experience?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my reports that were shown during my testimony last week, you can find one passage where it says in the beginning of 1998 citizens were very dissatisfied. Comments such as, What is the police doing and what is the army doing, were common because terrorists from day to day, from month to month kept taking up more and more territory and more and more roads so that citizens could no longer move freely.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would now like to show you 2D372, it's a letter from the Municipal Assembly -- to the Municipal Assembly of Orahovac. 8th July 1998 is the date. As we can see, this document says that among Serb citizenry there is confusion, fear, and despair because they're totally unprotected and in danger. With every passing day the terrorists move their lines closer to these villages, which are in fact surrounded. Do you remember that the misgivings expressed in this letter turned out to be justified very soon afterwards?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, nine days after this letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happened nine days after this letter?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nine days later, on the 17th of July, terrorists captured Orahovac, Zociste, Opterusa, and Retimlje. From Opterusa and Retimlje they kidnapped a large number of civilian Serbs and a large number of them were recorded as missing for a long time. We know nowadays that those men were killed, and it was through the mediation of international representatives based in Pristina that a number of women and children from these villages were later released. Orahovac was in the hands of the terrorists on the 17th and 18th of July, before it was liberated on the 19th and recovered as our territory under the control of MUP forces and army forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did your unit, together with the MUP, participate in the deblocking of Orahovac and pushing back of the terrorists?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My unit was the only one that participated in providing support to the MUP in this anti-terrorist operation, it was one of the first anti-terrorist operations in which a large settlement, a town practically, of 20 to 30.000 population had to be freed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the KLA forces and the resistance they put up made it impossible for the MUP to solve this problem on its own, alone?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this was too large an assignment for the MUP units that were on that territory at that time, and that they needed the support and the assistance of the army. That's the gist of the order I received from my commander, to support MUP forces that moved free this town again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would now like to move to another subject, the sector of state security as part of the MUP of Serbia. We heard already that you had good cooperation with SUP chiefs in 1998 and 1999. In 1998 it was Colonel Zekavica, and in 1999 it was with Colonel Vojnovic. Let me ask you, do you remember who was the chief of the centre of RDB, state security sector, and what was your relationship with that sector?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That sector was headed by Colonel Savic. We did not have frequent contacts. Our contacts were, in fact, rare. It was my security officer who was in touch with him more frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me now ask you, did you notice that between the SUP and the state security sector one of them is subordinated to the other, or were they sectors on an equal footing within one and the same ministry?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was no subordination between them; however, the state security sector was rather special and that's why I communicated more with the superior officers and chiefs of secretariats who were in charge of public security.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me now move to the next area, also rather brief. The reason is that we are trying to refute evidence given by K-79. When you spoke about anti-terrorist operations of the army and the police, you said that tanks were used selectively. My question might seem ridiculous to you, but I have to put it. Who was the tank crew, policemen or soldiers?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course it was always soldiers who formed a tank crew. It could never be policemen, and I have never heard that in any situation whatsoever policemen manned a tank.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could a chief of the police order a tank gunner to target a certain objective or not?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This request had to go through a -- from a lower-ranking policemen on the spot to the detachment commander; from the detachment commander to me; and the executive order had to be given by me, going down to the unit to which the tank belonged. And the commanding officer next to the tank had to size-up the target and decide whether it was necessary to open fire or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Let's move on to our next topic. We have another five minutes before the break. I would like to discuss the civilians leaving the country. When you testified on Thursday you spoke about the laying of mines and you mentioned it earlier today --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the page number.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- you said ground leading to the border was mined, and one lane was free for passage. You mentioned an incident when a police vehicle and one passenger vehicle entered the area that was mined and people were killed or injured. In connection with I would like to show you a Defence exhibit, 5D891, it's an exhibit of the Lazarevic Defence. We'll have it on the screen soon. It's your document. I'd like to ask you, that lane, was it mined up to the border crossing itself?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both lanes were mined in the beginning, and then the right lane was demined later. The lanes were mined on a stretch of 20 metres close to the border only. The rest of the road was not mined except in the area of the bridge and in the area of Zur village, where the road was mined but the entire road because the explosive was laid in mine drill-holes next to the road, so from the border to Zur village.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is true of Vrbnica border crossing. What about Cafa Prusit?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that anyone who was leaving Serbia to go to Albania via Kosovo and Metohija could do it only through border crossings, Vrbnica and Cafa Prusit, they were official state border crossings?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These two border crossings, however, there was some attempts to cross the border outside these border crossings, but those were attempts by armed groups who sometimes had civilians with them. And they tried to cross the border in other places to go to Albania, but these were the two official border crossings and civilians crossed the border legally according to their own wishes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If army units engaged in the defence of the border should see civilians trying to cross the state border, they would direct them to official crossings, wouldn't they? We're talking only about civilians.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course they would be stopped because other sections of the border were also mined, such as gaps between units. If they were in the border belt, they would be stopped, their papers would be checked, their personal details noted down, and if they were ordinary civilians they would be directed back to the roads leading either to Prizren or to Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. It's time for the break. We'll have to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, could you again please leave the courtroom with the usher, and we will resume at 1.45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.45 p.m.,

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] Could we please have in e-court Exhibit 5D885.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, as you can see, this is a document from the command of the 549th Brigade. In the first paragraph under number 1, the third sentence, or rather, the third line right there at the middle of it, it says: According to our information, between the 24th of March and the 2nd of April, around 290.000 people crossed the border at Vrbnica village and plus another 20.000 to 25.000 at Cafa Prusit. My question is: Did you have any information about the general number of people leaving after that date?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not precise information, but I did have some information. This is the information that was obtained from MUP, because at the border crossing itself there was the border police and the customs officials so that I did have the approximate figure for the people who crossed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. The next topic that I would like to ask you about has to do with the military territorial detachments. When you were talking about military territorial detachments, you said that once they were resubordinated to you they were sent to the border. These military territorial detachments, who were they subordinate to before they were resubordinated to you?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military territorial detachments were linked with the military departments. In my case it was the military department in Prizren. The Prizren military department was in turn subordinate to the Pristina military district.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And who was the Pristina military district subordinated to?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military district in Pristina was subordinated to, as were all the others, it was subordinated to the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that there was a mistake. Is it correct that the military district in Pristina was subordinated to the 3rd Army Nis, so we are not talking about civilian defence we are talking about the military territorial detachments?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The Pristina Military District was subordinated to the Nis army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will now read you -- read some numbers to you and I will ask you if these military territorial detachments were in the area of your responsibility. So 108th Military Territorial Detachment Prizren?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was in my area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The 70th Military Territorial Detachment Suva Reka?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 70th Military Territorial Detachment was subordinated only at the end of the war, as the war drew to the -- its close.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will come to the date of their resubordination. I just want you to confirm whether they were in your area. 101st Orahovac Military Territorial Detachment?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not subordinated to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 68th Military Territorial Detachment Gora?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that territorial detachment was subordinated to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 113th Military Territorial Detachment from Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just one company from the 113th Military Territorial Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the strength of the military territorial detachments ranged between 400 to 500 people?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have in e-court Exhibit P1925.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, we can see here that this is a document from the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army. It was sent to the command of the 3rd Army where it says: "I hereby order," we have numbers 1.3 and 1.4. We can see that this pertains to the 113th Military Territorial Detachment of Djakovica and the military territorial detachment from Suva Reka. And in item 3 we can see that the start of the mobilisation was set for the 25th of March, 1999, at 0000 hours. In practice did this mobilisation begin and was it carried out on that date, if you know; if you don't know --

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know that because they were not subordinate to me at that time, and I don't have any direct knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you. The Prizren Military Territorial Detachment and the Orahovac Military Territorial Detachment were resubordinated to you on the 9th of April, 1999; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Orahovac Military Territorial Detachment -- well, there are several orders on resubordination. If I may be allowed to have a look at them because it was first attached to another unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I'm sorry. It was resubordinated to the 252nd Brigade. Well, lest -- there are several documents I can show you but perhaps we can do it even without the documents. Do you agree with me that the tasks of the military territorial detachments, MTDs, were first of all to protect the population; second, to secure the buildings; third, to establish combat control of the territory, to destroy and rout the Siptar terrorist forces; and fourth, to counter any landing operations?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these might be their tasks, but that would depend on the territory where they actually were. Depending on that, some tasks came to the fore. For instance, in my area, securing the state border on some axes was their main task, that was for the 68th, the 113th, and the 108th Military Territorial Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that the command of the military district at the beginning of the war and until such time when those detachments were resubordinated to other units in fact set the tasks for MTDs, that you did not do that until such time when they were resubordinated to you?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite natural. They were linked with the military district, they reported to the military district, they received their orders from the military district. And from the time when we were actually resubordinated to me, I issued tasks to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we agree then that most of these MTDs, up until the time when they were resubordinated to other units, were actually located in inhabited areas or next to some roads?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know that -- I know that that was the case in particular with the 108th and the 68th MTD. The 68th MTD was mobilised in Dragas, and immediately after the mobilisation it was resubordinated to me around about that time. It was immediately tasked with manning a part of the state border. As far as the 108th MTD is concerned, for a brief period of time it was there close to Prizren on the Prizren-Brezovica road, and then later on for the most part it manned the border with the Republic of Macedonia and some smaller elements, including the command and the staff units, secured the Prizren-Suva Reka road.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know where the 70th MTD, the Suva Reka MTD was located?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 70th Suva Reka MTD, as I've already said, was resubordinated to me at the very end of the war. I know that it was also in the area around Suva Reka and that it was securing Suva Reka according to that map. I don't know what roads, but from the direction of Budakovo, in those areas where the terrorist forces were concentrated.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know where 101st Orahovac MTD was located?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the 101st MTD is concerned, it was never resubordinated to me. I don't know where it was actually stationed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what about 113th Djakovica MTD, the rest of it except for the one company that was resubordinated to you?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know that the company that was resubordinated to me was immediately sent to the state border, and it had its own defence sector on the state border. As for the rest of this MTD, I don't have any particular knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please assist us if you remember. What kind of uniforms did members of the MTDs wear?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Members of the MTDs wore M-77 uniforms. Only the command and the active element wore M-89 uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what was the age of the members in MTDs?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, their age was the same as the people who were sent to my unit. It would be natural to expect the older people to be in MTDs and the younger people to be in my unit, but they were mostly the same age approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, can you tell us their age --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before you do that. Your previous answer was translated: "Members of the MTDs wore M-77 uniforms. Only the command and the active element wore M-89 uniforms." Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is the active element?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that would be the personnel that was in the detachment in peacetime, or rather, not in the detachment, but in the military department. Military department had about 20 personnel officers and so on, and they wore those newer uniforms and everybody else wore the older uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. And you're being asked to tell us the age of the membership of the MTDs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, between 25, so people who had just done their national service, and up until the age of 40 for the most part, maybe drivers and some other specialists or cooks, something like that, they would be older than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Could you please tell us what kind of weapons the MTDs had.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as infantry weapons are concerned, they had the same weapons as we did. In platoons, companies, they would have automatic rifles, light machine-guns, machine-guns. Only as far as the support weapons are concerned, they would have nothing heavier than 82-millimetre mortars, nothing heavier than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us what kind of vehicles they used.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't have their own vehicles. Those were vehicles from the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain to us, what does that mean, vehicles from the list?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, just as the personnel, vehicles from some companies were listed in mobilisation lists. And when you mobilise people, you mobilise vehicles from those companies too, sometimes together with the drivers; and they are then used up until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So these vehicles would not be marked as police or military vehicles?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They had their normal licence plates and they only bore a sign that was set in order to indicate that this vehicle had been mobilised or requisitioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did MTDs have their military police?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Military territorial detachments did not have a military police, but the military department command did have a platoon of a military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your clarification. Members of the MTDs are members of the Army of Yugoslavia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd now like to ask you something else, something about the anti-terrorist actions. With regard to the one that began on the 25th of March, 1999, Retimlje, that action, you said that you received an order by courier from the Pristina Corps and that on the basis of that order you issued your own order in turn. Now, the order, in addition to the other documents, did you receive a decision map, or rather, a map by which this action should be conducted?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did receive part of that large map, the sector applying to my brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do apologise, my question was not precise enough. That's what I meant. Anyway, did that map have the axis and deployment of the MUP units that you received from your superior command?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, I think it did contain which MUP units would take part in my area but without the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You explained to us the way in which you coordinated with MUP with respect to planning and executing the anti-terrorist actions in 1998 and 1999. First of all, with the example of Jeskovo for the 9th of March, 1999, and the document is P2067. We don't have to have it up on e-court, but anyway it says that parts of the 37th Detachment and the Prizren company took part PJP company took part jointly. Do you remember where you conducted the coordination with the MUP officers pursuant to your order to destroy the Retimlje STS, the terrorist forces?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The coordination was done pursuant to the order [as interpreted], or rather, we conducted coordination before I wrote the order and we coordinated in the office of the chief of the secretariat of the MUP in Prizren, where he called upon the commander of the 37th Detachment and the commander of I think it was the 5th Company of the PJP of Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, with your leave, we have an error in transcript, page 81, line 6, the coordination was done pursuant to an order. Witness said completely opposite. That was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's what I heard as well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, you had a meeting with the MUP representatives in the SUP of Prizren before you wrote your order. Now, on that occasion at that meeting, were the tasks of all the units precisely defined and indeed the Army of Yugoslavia and the MUP?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the extent -- in the extent to which that was necessary for everyone to know what their assignment and task was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And this anti-terrorist action, did it take place in keeping with what you decided upon together with the representatives of the MUP and your general coordination with them?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was implemented within the planned time and as we had planned it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You've already testified about this, but we of course are interested in seeing if anything can be added.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So may on e-court we have Exhibit P1995, please. We need --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Or rather, this is an analysis of you of the actions of the 549th Motorised Brigade to destroy the Siptar terrorist forces in the Retimlje-Suva Reka-Orahovac of the 30th of March, 1999, and we need page 2 in B/C/S, point 2, para 6. And it begins with the words: "During the first day ..." Can you see that, General?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say that on that first day the immediate task was realized --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think it must be the next page for the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I didn't have time because I planned to do it this morning to find references in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We have it now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say that on that first day the immediate task was realized -- "on the first day the immediate task was achieved and that the forces of the 23rd PJP made a first break through from the village of Bela Crkva and Brnjaca towards the village of Celina and Mala Hoca." Could you please now show us on the map, or rather, draw in that axis, the PJP's breakthrough. Have you remembered the axis, General?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On e-court could we have the next exhibit, it is P615, page 22. Can we zoom in. One more time, please. Now can we see the lower portion of the map. Thank you. Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So that we can have a good overview, let's use different colours. So for MUP would you please use the green pen. Do you need any assistance?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you draw on the map the axis that we said the forces of the 23rd Detachment of the PJP took in their movement and when they broke through, Bela Crkva-Brnjaca towards the village of Celina and Mala Hoca.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have a slight problem here, there's no green pen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, then we can use the red one.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the area that you mentioned of the 23rd Detachment. It started out from that direction. Now the second part of the 23rd Detachment went this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you arrived in Celina between 5.00 and 7.00 hours. There was no fighting in Bela Crkva, let's say that first?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no fighting in Bela Crkva.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My colleague Mr. Cepic would like to say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We heard the assertion made here, or rather, my colleague said that the general said that he entered at Celina between 5 and 7 hours so may I have a reference for that kind of statement. I don't think I've heard that so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, when did you enter Bela Crkva?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I entered Bela Crkva a little after 5.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you go into Celina?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I passed by Celina along the asphalt road to Zrze and then I entered Bela Crkva, saw my commander, the commander of the 2nd Motorised Battalion, and then I continued on to Orahovac to my point at Mount Milenica, the Kraz [phoen] facility, the Kraz feature.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That was my mistake. Now, along that axis you said that your Combat Group 2 took the same direction. So use another colour apart from red and draw that in, please. Show us with Combat Group 2 moved.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Combat Group 2 moved along this way, I'll draw it in blue, the same way as the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, at the Slobodan Milosevic trial, Vukovic, the commander of Combat Group 2, said that the police entered Bela Crkva first and then Combat Group 2 followed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we have a page reference for that if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, I don't have the reference, but I can ask the General.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you know who entered Bela Crkva first, General?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived - and that was at around 5.00 --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said you just passed by Bela Crkva?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw my commander there and my soldiers were already passing through Bela Crkva towards Amovac hill. I myself, I don't remember that I saw the police in that part, the policemen that I had seen earlier on along the road from Prizren towards Bela Crkva. I didn't see any police there, possibly they came but later on, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you were moving from Prizren -- well, you said you met them. Had they already passed Bela Crkva because you were coming from the top and they were coming from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 23rd Detachment was supposed to come from Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Oh, I see, Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I came from Zrze myself, so it means Prizren, Zrze, and then I moved towards Orahovac. Now, along the road, along the way, in Pirane I saw my unit and along the communication line I also saw part of my forces who had already arrived at the blockade line. They were up on the asphalt road, and that's where I noticed that there was some police there, but I don't know to which units they belonged. It is possible that it might have been a detachment from the -- company from the 23rd Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I'm not going to ask you to do guess-work. If you don't know, that's fine. You didn't happen to see that in Bela Crkva somebody was setting fire to any houses or anything like that taking place?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was nothing, no activities, in Bela Crkva; there was just the barking of dogs, that's all you can hear, and the army passed by, quite normally, through Bela Crkva towards the eastern side where Amovac hill is located, which we were -- they were supposed to take control of.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. That completes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd just like an IC number for the map that's on e-court now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC154, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Hannis for the Prosecution. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'd like to fill in a little bit of your background that I don't think we heard about on your direct testimony. Can you tell us just the years that you were in the army, from when to when?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the 20th of July, 1977, until the 31st of March, 2005.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what rank did you hold when you retired?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major-general.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You had something just under 30 years when you retired; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you calculate it, it is around about 30 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Why did you retire at that time? Wasn't that a little bit early?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not retire of my own will. I was pensioned off.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who did that? Who pensioned you off? Who made that decision?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That decision was made by the Supreme Defence Council on the 24th of December, 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who were the members at that time?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president of Serbia, Mr. Tadic; the president of the federal state, Mr. Marovic; and from Montenegro, there was Mr. Vujanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You, I recall from reading your testimony in the Milosevic trial, am I correct that you reached the rank of colonel at a very young age. You were actually the youngest colonel in the VJ at the time you achieved that rank, correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one of the youngest, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And likewise, I think I read or heard it said that you were -- when you reached the rank of general, you were the youngest general in the VJ?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: To me as an outsider, it seems that you were on the fast track, if I can use that term, and it's surprising to me that you were pensioned off before your 30 years. Do you have -- can you help us with why that happened. You said that that wasn't voluntary, that you didn't want to go that soon. Do you know why?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was never explained to me, although I did ask for an explanation, and before the Supreme Court of Serbia proceedings are still underway because I appealed the decision to pension me off because it was not done in a lawful manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you have any theories yourself? You must have some idea?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that this question calls for speculation on the witness's part because, if I may --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel misspoke and said "client's part."

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness explained that there were legal proceedings under way so any imposition of an answer would be pure speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We disagree with you, Mr. Cepic. We think the witness is in a position to tell us if he is aware of anything or suspects anything that may be the reason for this. So could you answer the question, please, Mr. Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry to also interfere, but he would be having some plea before the Supreme Court and he can explain that plea. I mean, if the matter is sub juris, it makes no difference. The plea that you have taken before the Supreme Court as to why you were prematurely with such a brilliant background.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, it was the Supreme Court of Serbia and Montenegro; however, it didn't take up the legal proceedings when the state community separated into two independent states. Then the case came to the Supreme Court of Serbia, but to the present day not a single sitting was held, no session was held, and it was never discussed or has not been discussed to date. So through my lawyers all I managed to do was to learn that the case was before the Supreme Court, but no scheduling for any session has yet been made. The pensioning off was certainly a surprise to me, came as a surprise to me, because in that year, 2004, I had conducted the largest exercise in the last 20 years in Serbia and Montenegro which was excellently reviewed and it was with the Army of Romania, and I received a decoration that year. I received all manner of commendations. And I asked for an explanation, and I reached the minister of defence; however, he said that he did not have the power to tell me the reason for my having been pensioned off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: The question remains: What -- if you put in a petition before the Supreme Court or an appeal before the Supreme Court, you must have taken some grounds. I think that is -- that -- those become important.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I set out all the grounds, and according to none of the legal grounds should I have been pensioned off. There were no legal grounds to pension me off. I hadn't reached the age required, I hadn't done my years of service necessary for a pension. I had 35 years of service at the time, whereas the pension requires 40 years of service, pensionable service. I was 48 years old at the time, and generals with my rank are usually pensioned off when they're 57, so that no -- none of those grounds had been fulfilled. And the real reason -- I was never given the real reason because the President of Serbia, Mr. Tadic, did not want to receive me, did not wish to talk to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, I share your surprise, and you mentioned speaking to the minister of defence and being told that he didn't have the power to tell you and trying to talk to President Tadic. But you must have talked to some of your colleagues, your fellow generals, about it, did you not?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
