utterances.text: I looked at a document while I was still in active service when an admiral from the US was visiting. At that time, after year 2000, the so-called democratic forces came into power in Serbia, and one of the demands was that all generals from Milosevic's time be pensioned off.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So is that -- do you think that's the reason that you got pensioned off, because of that demand?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only guess. All I know is that I was pensioned off illegally. I had not reached a single limit for going into retirement. I had requested an interview with the president of Serbia and with the minister of defence, but I was received only by the minister. That president of the state union of Serbia and Montenegro said that he had voted for my pensioning off because the president of Serbia had asked him to do so. A consensus is needed for that kind of decision. As for Montenegrin generals, that was decided by the president of Montenegro. And in such occasions he asked for the vote of the president of Serbia, because as I said, the consensus was required in decisions like promotions, demotions, et cetera, pensions. And there was a lot of speculation about that, but I do not want to go into it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But not all of the generals from Milosevic's time were pensioned off when you were, were they?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most were, others were pensioned off the next year, the following year.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But hadn't most of those met the retirements for pensioning off, unlike you?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was pensioned off, it was in a group of another 11 generals. Out of those 11, perhaps two or three had reached the age limit and the maximum years of service. Others, apart from those three, had the required years of service. I did not meet either requirement, age or years of service.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That doesn't make sense in English again. You said, according to the English, that out of 11, perhaps two or three had reached the age limit and the maximum years of service. Others, apart from those three, had the required years of service. So there were three different bases on which they qualified for pension; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are two in fact. Three met both requirements, they had enough years of age and full years of service; others had full years of service but not the age limit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, it's my understanding that General Dikovic, who was commander of the 37th Brigade during Kosovo, is still active duty, correct? So he wasn't pensioned off?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said all the generals who became generals under Milosevic were pensioned off. Dikovic became a general later.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you: What have you done since you left the army in 2005? I understand you're now a member of the parliament or the National Assembly, correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but in the Assembly of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when did you get elected to that position?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was elected an MP in January, or rather, the elections were in January, and I became an MP in February when the Assembly was formed. Later I was also elected vice-president of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, I understood that you were deputy speaker or vice-president. How many deputy speakers are there? Is there only one? Are you the only one or are there more than one?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The Assembly of Serbia has six vice-presidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And I understand you're a member of the Serb Radical Party, Mr. Seselj's party, correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I take it you support the nationalistic views of that party?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, it's a democratic party, the Serb Radical Party, and I would like to hear from you what you mean by nationalist or nationalistic. The Serb Radical Party is certainly a patriotic party that loves its people, but nowadays, together with the Socialist Party of Serbia, it is the only real democratic party that has national interests at heart.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me move on to military instead of politics. You took up your command of the 549th as I understand in 1998; is that right? When did you first take command of the 549th?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that was in 1997, in the month of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how did you get appointed to that position? Who put you there?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the 549th Brigade I was from the 6th of February, 1995, on the position of Chief of Staff. From 2nd September 1996 until 26 July 1997, I was in training at the School of National Defence; and after that training I returned to the unit where, pursuant to an order of the Chief of General Staff, I was appointed commander. And my predecessor, Colonel Kuzmanovic was transferred to Belgrade because he had been commander for a long time before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. We'll talk about the School of National Defence in a thesis you wrote there a little later on, but I want to ask you about some of the answers you gave on Wednesday of last week, on your first day of testimony. You mentioned that in 1998, when there were incidents at the border - this is in the early part of 1998 - an investigative judge would come to the scene and crime scene technicians would come. And at that time there was a local mixed commission which would also be summoned from our organs and from Albania. But you said: "Sometime in May, after that, the contact ceased and the local mixed commissions from Albania refused to come." What happened that made that change? Do you know why the mixed commission members from Albania stopped coming when incidents happened at the border?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In May during the -- an incident when a local mixed commission from the Yugoslav and the Albanian side, terrorists were firing from the side of Albania and from the Albanian side, and they did not allow the on-site investigation to proceed normally. The Albanian member of that mixed commission said that he could not hold or keep those terrorists under control and that he could not guarantee anybody's safety or security while the on-site investigation was going on. At that time it is common knowledge that the army and the police were in a state of chaos and disintegration, in Albania. After that incident, on-site investigations were only attended by our authorities. If anyone was killed, the investigating judge from Nis would also come. And very often at an on-site investigation, if it was taking place on the border, it was under fire from Albanian territory and the persons performing the investigation were jeopardized.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I want to ask you about something that's in one of your orders dated the 18th of June, 1998, this is Exhibit 5D859.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could call that up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: There's a reference to something that's been translated into English as "indirectly recruited soldiers." And I don't see the English on the screen to direct you to the point, but it's talking about the preparedness of indirectly recruited soldiers. Can you find that, General? I'm not sure which item it's in.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That term is absolutely inadequate. Could you just tell me which paragraph to look at?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, General, I don't have the English --

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it, I found it, para 4. It says: "Soldiers from," literally "indirect," but in fact it's "emergency mobilisation." Those were soldiers who were mobilised on the territory of Kosovo and Metohija and attached to our unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And when was this emergency mobilisation ordered, if you know?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not about a mobilisation. If I am allowed to read the entire paragraph, then it might be clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you do, Mr. Cepic has an intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, with your leave, error in translation. No one mentioned "mobilisation," and we had that word on page 95, line 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think the best plan, Mr. Delic, is that you read that paragraph, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We do not have one-to-one equivalency between Serbian and English. This is a term that is translated as "emergency recruitment" or "mobilisation."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "In all units of the brigade, continue with morale and psychological preparations, focusing on soldiers from emergency recruitment. Unprepared soldiers from emergency recruitment or mobilisation should not be assigned to independent assignments or obligations."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, General, there may be -- I understand from the interpreter's comments that there's not a one-to-one translation between the term in Serbian and the term in English. So if you could explain to me -- it sounds like these are soldiers that are coming up not in the regular course somehow. Could you explain to me when and how that happened.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, I have already said at the very beginning of my testimony that perhaps until March 1998 we trained our own soldiers in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. After that, however, due to the complexity of the situation, soldiers were trained in centres outside Kosovo and Metohija, in Valjevo, in Pirot, and in Podgorica. After completed training, they would come to my unit; that's why they were called "indirectly recruited."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you allow me, my English is not perfect, but I believe faulty interpretation caused part of this problem. I think, however, this last answer explains more correctly what is meant as opposed to "emergency recruitment."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Whatever term we use, is this some supplemental complement of additional soldiers that you normally would not have had but for the exceptional circumstances at the time?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Hannis. These are soldiers that would certainly belong to me while they were doing their military service, but instead of serving with me from day one they would complete their basic training outside of Kosovo and Metohija and come to me to serve the rest of their term. They were within the normal complement that my brigade should have.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And why weren't they trained in Kosovo then? Was it because of the circumstances existing in Kosovo, that it was not safe to be training in there?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely, it was not safe, because on their way to the training grounds they could get into some sort of danger.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right, General, I want to ask you about what Mr. Fila told you was one of my favourite topics, and that's the Joint Command. Do you recall the first time you heard that term, "Joint Command", used in Kosovo in connection with the VJ and the MUP?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime in 1998, the summer of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We have an exhibit, 5D841, which I believe there's not an English translation in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But, Your Honours, I would indicate to you it's my understanding there is an English translation from the Milosevic case. It was tab 66 of Exhibit D300. I don't know if we're going to be able to find that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But, General, could you look at the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The existence of that means that the translation of the exhibit does not need to be repeated, and that could be loaded into e-court as the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour. I only found out about it recently, and this was a 5D exhibit and I didn't know if it was going to be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, this is dated the 7th of July, 1998. Do you recognise it? This is an order from you.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's an order from my brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the gist of it, as I understand, is you are ordering your subordinate units that no action should be taken on the ground without your prior knowledge; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you issue this order based on order that you had received from the Pristina Corps command, and I think that's the item number 1104-6, dated the 6th of July, referred to in the first line of text, correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, I believe that that document from the Pristina Corps actually made reference to the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija. Do you recall that? I don't have the document in front of me, but I have other reason to think that and I'll show you in a minute. But I wanted to ask you if you recall that.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember this order of mine very clearly; however, the order of the Pristina Corps which served as a basis for mine I no longer remember, although it must have arrived in my unit. Because I usually did not allow for this Joint Command to be written to avoid confusing my COs. I always used the heading "command of the Pristina Corps," regardless of their heading. Maybe I was not around when my operations officer wrote this order, so it went out like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, if we could look at the bottom of the page or the last page if it's more than one, that's your signature, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. This order is on one page only.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And it's signed by you. Could you go to the top and read that line for me, because now I see the English and it does appear to make a reference to Joint Command. Could you read that first line. "Pursuant to the order ..."

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Pursuant to the order of the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija, strictly confidential number 1104-6, dated 6 July 1998, and bearing in mind past experiences in performing combat actions as well as the damage suffered by units as a result of poorly prepared and poorly performed actions, and with a view to increasing efficiency in the execution of tasks at all levels and achieving better organization and cooperation with units in the area of responsibility, I hereby order ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I see with the help of my case manager we now have that in e-court and on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So, General, I take it this may have been the first time that you had seen that term, right, around July 6th, 1998?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's written there and I absolutely am not trying to dispute that I received this order of the Pristina Corps on the 6th, and somewhere in that order it is written "Joint Command," I don't know exactly where -- or maybe I received it in the form of telegram.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My question to you, though, is a similar question. I've asked several other military witnesses here. It seems to me as a soldier the word "command" has certain significance greater than it may have for a non-military person. And as I understand it, Joint Command is not a body that is provided for in the Law on Defence, et cetera. Didn't it arouse your curiosity when you saw a document with this name in capital letters "Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija"? Didn't you wonder what that was or who that was?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To me as a commanding officer, it is the contents that matters. In terms of its essence and contents, this is a completely military order that regulates some basic issues. Perhaps, as I said, at that moment I didn't even notice this wording "Joint Command," but of course I had an interest in it. I knew that in Pristina there was a forward command post of the 3rd Army, that General Simic was there, that certain elements of the air force and air defence were there as well, and my thinking went along those lines, that it was written because -- because there are some three army levels, part of the army command, part of the military command, and part of yet another structure that does not belong to ground forces. But from my viewpoint as a commander on a tactical level and for the purposes of the order that I was supposed to draft, that was of absolutely no consequence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, General, I beg to disagree with you. You said for you what was important was the contents, but I say to you as a military man, it's also important who the message comes from. Because if some sergeant had sent you an order, you would certainly treat it differently than if you had an order from your colonel or your general, right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is defined in the army who is supposed to issue orders and who is not. Of course I can receive orders only from my superiors. This order came from my superior command, the Pristina Corps. It's just a heading that I read out. The only part in dispute here is the term, "Joint Command," but everything else that is listed in those items 1 through 7 is completely, completely clear and is absolutely not at dispute at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't disagree with you about that. It just strikes me as strange that you would not inquire, that you wouldn't contact General Pavkovic or his Chief of Staff and say, What's this Joint Command? I never heard of it before. Where did that come from? Who is that? Why is that my order? None of those questions came to your mind? You didn't inquire?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in those days I talked to General Pavkovic every morning, and General Pavkovic came to visit my unit very frequently, but that may be one of the rare orders where it says "Joint Command." In almost all or the vast majority of the orders, it would say the Pristina Corps command. And when I sent in reports or when General Pavkovic inquired after the status of my unit, he never mentioned any Joint Command because there was this direct relationship between me as his subordinate and General Pavkovic as the commander or General Lazarevic as the Chief of Staff, who also had the right to issue orders to me. And during that time-period he was in Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And after the time that General Pavkovic got promoted to head up the 3rd Army and later on became Chief of the General Staff, did you ever have any conversations with him? Did you ever discuss Joint Command with him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, Mr. Hannis, but it is something similar to your objection. Your Honours, could you please bear in mind that this is the 6th of July, this -- 1998, this is the time when there are no civilians, according to the Prosecution evidence. And when I showed the document from the 23rd of March, I was criticised for showing a document that preceded the air-strikes. This is the 6th of July. This is the time before the -- this period. So could you please bear that in mind. There are no civilians on the 6th of July, and could you please look at the log number, 1104. So I'm afraid that the Trial Chamber is being misled here. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I don't think Mr. Hannis has mentioned civilians in this context, have you?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, and actually we have a document that's a response to an RFA that indicates that the Joint Command was formed I believe earlier than the 6th or 7th of July, but that's not the point I'm trying to make here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But what we're dealing with here is a document in which the Joint Command is mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now my question is, General, you mentioned speaking with General Pavkovic on almost a daily basis in 1998, when he was commander of the Pristina Corps, correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were daily reports that I was supposed to make every morning. I was supposed to call the commander every morning and report to him about the status of my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And during those daily reports, there was never any mention or discussion of the Joint Command; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Joint Command was never mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At some point in time, though, you must have learned that Joint Command was an important or a controversial issue here in The Hague Tribunal. You were asked about it and questioned about it when you testified in the Milosevic trial, correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Have you ever had any discussion with General Pavkovic about the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not discuss this with General Pavkovic; I discussed it with my colleagues at the same level. Again, I asked them when they heard about it and whether they knew what this term, "Joint Command," actually meant. But as I said in 2005 at the Milosevic trial, I did not change my opinion. Had any kind of Joint Command existed, it would have had a commander, and in those two years I would have seen this man, what he looked like. I think that this is just an unfortunate term that was used in order to organize the coordination between the MUP and the army, and that this was its sole purpose. As a soldier, I do know what every kind of command means. For any body to call itself a command, it has to have certain elements. To give you an example, I never saw a stamp of the Joint Command. I never saw any log number in an order that would be a log number of a command of this sort because it would have to have its office, it would have to have its registry. The numbers were always those of the Pristina Corps, they would also be in the Pristina Corps registry, and I was never asked, nor did I do that on anyone's orders. I never reported to anything called the Joint Command. If I had to, if I had to report to a Joint Command, I would have been in a big difficult situation because it didn't have an office, it didn't have a telephone number. I always reported to my commander, the corps commander, or his Chief of Staff. And this whole Joint Command quandary actually cropped up in 2005 when I first came to the Tribunal to testify in the Milosevic case, where the Prosecutor, Mr. Nice, asked me several times about the Joint Command; and my reply was more or less the one I gave you now. I, as the brigade commander, consider that the other units that participated in an action - and those would be the MUP units - cannot get an order with the heading "the Pristina Corps" because they would be unwilling to take part in that activity, just as I would be unwilling to provide support to any MUP units if I received an order from the MUP staff or anyone else for that matter --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- but when it says "the Joint Command, when I receive it from my command, from the Pristina Corps command, when I get this from a courier and when my commander informs me that I should participate in this action and that I should prepare my unit, then there's nothing controversial about it because I have only my commander above me and I am not interested in anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I'll try and find the precise reference, but today I thought you answered a question and said something in that regard that the use of the Joint Command you thought was primarily so that MUP would go along with what was being directed. Why would MUP follow an order that was headed "Joint Command"?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't fully agree with your statement. I, as a commander, understood it in the following way. There in Pristina at the corps level and at the level of the Pristina MUP, I don't know whether it was the MUP staff or whatever, that was where the first coordination was done, and an agreement was reached at that level that we at the lower levels, the brigade commanders, should participate in a joint activity. And that -- to that end it was necessary for the same order because I as the brigade commander get the same order as the secretariat chief or the commander of a MUP detachment. So for this direct coordination to be carried out and for us to be able to carry out this coordinated action, the only to do it was to do it this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, are you saying that you knew that the MUP and the VJ were meeting in Pristina, or are you just speculating about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was in Pristina maybe twice. It was in July, or rather, in August, maybe August and September when we received orders for some of those activities that were part of the five-stage plan, so I was in Pristina on two occasions. And I know that I received an order at that time and that the secretariat chief and the detachment commander who participated with me in the coordinated action received their orders on the same day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you've said a moment ago: "There in Pristina at corps level and at the level of the Pristina MUP, I don't know whether it was the MUP staff or whatever, that was where the first coordination was done, and an agreement was reached at that level." Now, if you have knowledge of that, can you tell us who were the personnel reaching agreement at that level?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I never attended those coordination meetings. On that occasion where I was there to receive those documents, Mr. Pavkovic was there and some other people from the corps command, Mr. Lukic, and some other people from the MUP in Pristina. Some of the brigade commanders that were part of the Pristina Corps, the commanders of the MUP detachments, I can't tell you their number now, but I'm sure that this man who took part in the same activity as I did was there. And the chief of my secretariat in Prizren was also present there. But the coordination had already been done. We just got there. I think that the meeting was held in the MUP building in Pristina, and that's where we received the documents. That's where I saw this colleague from the MUP that would participate with me in that action. We got introduced to each other and we agreed about where we would meet in Prizren once we got back and where we would develop the coordination further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: On the point that Mr. Hannis is exploring with you, it would be helpful if you could give us a short, direct answer, because I don't think we have any documents - I'll be corrected if I'm wrong - I don't think we have any Joint Command-headed documents passing through the MUP system. And his question to you is: Why would a MUP officer respond better to a document headed "Joint Command" than he might otherwise do. Can you give us a clear and simple answer to that? It was your suggestion, after all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can give you an answer. For me it is completely acceptable. If I were a MUP officer it would be completely unacceptable to me if it contained the words "Pristina Corps command," but if it said "Joint Command," it would be acceptable because I would consider that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But what I don't think you're hearing from me is I don't think we have any such documents that say "Joint Command." So are you telling us that there's a whole series of documents in the MUP system with "Joint Command" on them that we've never seen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I cannot say that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: They're all --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- I cannot claim that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think they're all Pristina Corps documents. Is that wrong, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, all the ones that I'm aware of have the Pristina Corps 455 series number. There is one from I think General Lazarevic that is addressed to the head of MUP staff, but that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So there don't seem to be any of the documents you envisage, Mr. Delic, and we're left seeking an explanation for the use of this expression within the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why am I saying this? You mentioned some documents. There are 15 or more orders with the heading "Joint Command." They are all from 1999. I know that at those coordination meetings at MUP, or rather, when coordination was done with MUP, I know that the MUP commander received the very same document in his envelope. I had my own document that said the Joint Command with the very same number, and he got his own document and he had the same part of the map that I had, the same section of the map that I had. And that was the basis for our coordination. I don't know what happened with those documents and what is done with those documents in the MUP. Once the coordination planning was done, I made my own decision map and my order for my own units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you saying that he received a map which said "Pristina Corps" on it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It doesn't say "Pristina Corps" on the map; it said section of the map, for instance, detachment so-and-so. And for me it would say section for 549th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But I understand your evidence to be that it would get to him through his chain of command.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, definitely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, let me divide this up into two parts. First let me talk about 1998 because we don't have any -- we don't have any Joint Command orders with the 455 log-book number on them in 1998. But as I recall in your testimony in Milosevic you talked about the five-phase plan for combatting terrorism. Do you recall that? This is what I referred to as the summer offensive in 1998 between July and September/October 1998. Do you recall that five-phase plan?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I recall that I participated in a certain number of activities that were part of that plan, not in all five stages because they were not carried out in my territory, but in two or three of those I did participate with my unit, providing support to the MUP units.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I'll have to try and find the specific reference. If you tell me I'm wrong, I'll bring it in tomorrow. But I recall reading -- I think you said that before each phase -- before each phase you would go to Pristina and -- you and some of the other VJ commanders who were going to be involved in that phase, and you met with your MUP counterparts and the coordination was done then and there. Is that right? Is that what you said or is that how it happened?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, approximately, yes. I've already said that I participated in two or three activities that were part of the five-stage plan, and that's how many times I actually went to Pristina, the number of times that my unit was involved in this. But we were there not in order to carry out the actual coordination but to receive our orders because the coordination had already been completed in Pristina at a higher level, and then we developed this coordination at my place in the field. Most often we actually did it in the office of the MUP secretariat chief in Prizren. He would invite the commanders of the units, the MUP units that were supposed to participate in the activity, and I would go there as a representative of the army. And we would coordinate our activities there before I proceeded to actually draft the order for the activity. Because pursuant to the conclusions that were reached at that coordination meeting, I would draft my order and my operations officer would draw the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me be sure I understand the process. If some of your troops were going to be involved in a part of one of these phases of the plan for combatting terrorism in 1998, you and your MUP counterpart would go to Pristina and receive the orders; is that right so far?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it was not just the two of us because those stages required the participation of other units. So other commanders, both from the MUP and the army, would go there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who there in Pristina gave you those orders? Who handed them out to you? Was that General Pavkovic? Was that somebody from the operations staff? Was it -- do you recall?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. General Pavkovic was present, but some officer from the operations department in the Pristina Corps would distribute envelopes to us, envelopes containing the orders and the map sections for our respective units.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So is this similar to what you described in 1999, where we saw an envelope as an exhibit where you had received an order and a map, et cetera, except here you're in Pristina being handed it hand-to-hand. Is that right so far?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it's similar to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So you get an envelope and it has the order, it has a map or an excerpt of a map as well? Anything else in that envelope? You told us about these sort of separate orders for the engineering and artillery.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For engineering and artillery, not always. It would depend on where the artillery brigade was deployed and used. Sometimes you would get an order for artillery too and, when necessary, for the engineers too in the same envelope.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then was there a discussion then and there, in Pristina, about what you and your counterpart were going to do or did you go back to Prizren and work out the details there? How did that go?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, before the envelopes were distributed, General Pavkovic or General Lukic would address us briefly. They would describe the situation, the current situation on the ground vis-a-vis the terrorist forces in a certain sector. And then they would say that on such and such a date the activity should start. It was not termed "stage." There was some other term. It was given the name of the location, Drenica, Malisevo, or something of the sort. And then when the documents were distributed to us, then it was said that my unit, for instance, should go with a MUP unit, such and such a MUP unit. And the first time and maybe the second time I was there, since I had not seen these people at all before, I as the commander of my brigade would stand up and the man from the MUP would stand up; and at the end of this meeting we would meet and we would discuss -- because it would be indicated how much time we had until the start of the activity, one, two, or three days. And depending on that time-limit we would arrange a meeting at the secretariat chief's office in Prizren, and to specify the details, or rather, to coordinate this activity, how we should proceed on the ground in the area where we were to take part in the combat operations because there were other units there too. And I would talk only to the commander that my unit was supposed to support. Sometimes you would have two MUP commanders, but I was not interested in the others that were to be supported by other army units. I was only interested in those that I was supposed to support in this specific situation pursuant to that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, would this be an appropriate time to break for the day? I did have one procedural matter -- or actually two very brief ones I'd like to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We can deal with these in a moment. Mr. Delic, we need to bring today's proceedings to an end at this stage. We will resume tomorrow at 9.00. We will see you then. Can you please leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. There were two matters. On the 29th of August there were two redactions made during the testimony of a witness because I had some concerns there might be some national security implications for one country or another. I've determined that's not a problem and I would now move to open those up, it's the same name mentioned twice, Mr. Haider knows where they are. So I'd like to make that oral application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, we shall recall the redactions so that these now become part of the public transcript. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. The second thing, Your Honour, relates to Exhibit P950 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hannis, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The second relates to Exhibit P950, the interview of General Lazarevic. We have now completed a transcript which contains both the B/C/S and English. I would like to make an oral application to substitute it into e-court for the one that we previous had which only had English, and it's been disclosed to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. We will allow that also. So the effect of that is that there is a transcript of the whole of what's recorded on the videos, plus the videos, comprising that exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. The only thing that I have a concern about, Your Honour, is that when we discussed it when we had English only, I made a reference to page 73. Now with the inserted B/C/S the page number will be different, but I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does that not mean we should retain both?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Perhaps for ease of reference --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So in other words this should be added to the exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah, that's probably better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. That's the order we shall make.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There are two other matters that I'd like to address briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The first of these two other matters concerns the translation of exhibits for the Lukic Defence. There has been an e-mail exchange following the submission of the, I think, whole of the documents requiring translation, but there does seem to be still an absence of a priority list.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's not the case, Your Honour. Your Honour, we submitted those documents now multiple times with dates. When I put a date and I send a document, and I said that the date is in March, that means that that document is less of a priority than the document I sent for tomorrow or the next day. I don't see what kind of other list I can prepare. If I give a date that implies the priority for the document. I complied with the Court's order to submit all documents in this respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Give me an example of what you do that determines its priority.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. For instance, documents that are given a time-period of one to three days are documents that are going to be used for cross-examination of upcoming witnesses. Documents that are also considered to be high priority are pursuant to your Court's order that all MFI documents that have been previously admitted need to be submitted as high priority. Then we have-- so we have selected documents from our 65 ter list that relate to military documents that we intend to use with other military witnesses from the Defence -- from the other Defence case. Those are submitted as documents that we need within the next -- I think we have up to 1.5 months and then we have some documents that we foresee for the first third of our witnesses that are in the 1.5 to two-month period, so on and so on. So we have broken down the documents based upon what we foresee our Defence case is going to be. And I cannot sit there with the resources and the limited time that we have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That is an old refrain, Mr. Ivetic. We are particularly conscious that everybody is affected by that problem. The fact remains that these have to be put into a form that will enable them to be translated according to priority. Now, it seems to me from what you've said that there may be a breakdown in communication, and if that is the case it will be resolved later today. But you're saying that the priority is already clear in the submissions you've made?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. And every document that we submit or most of the documents that we submit, especially those from the 65 ter list we were very conscious to put in the reference section, the request section, precisely why -- which category why the document is being requested and if there was a possibility of moving the date if it was perhaps a longer document we have always stated in there the end date why that would be needed by for instance as Your Honour required the inquiry the other day about motions to admit documents from the bar table those documents have been bumped up in priority and have been specifically stated in the request in the electronic system these are a priority because of the need to have a motion to admit from the bar table sooner rather than later and that's why we've given most of those documents a date of no later than late January for translation which is what I represented to Your Honour the other day when that issue came up. So for each document I've signed a particular reason why it's been given the due date that's it's been given, and we've invited CLSS to change the date on their own prerogative given certain guidelines or contact us ASAP if it's a matter where we need a document as soon as possible for cross-examination or for other purposes that might need more explanation with them So, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now the other issue relating to these translations is the absence of a selection of representative documents. Was it not to be the case that you would try to select certain ones for translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, your order told me to put every document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The Prosecution were happy represented others.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Again CLSS is mixing documents. Those documents that we talked about in selection are not these documents we're talking about now. The documents that I submitted were documents from our 65 ter list of witnesses -- exhibits which Your Honours ordered me to do by the 30th. They're talking about documents that are overviews and we have certain other issues with respect to those given other rulings of the Chamber that I've sent CLSS and OLAD information on and I'm working with to see how we're going to handle some of the other documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're speaking too quickly for me, Mr. Ivetic. I thought that by now you were to have submitted everything for translation by the 30th of --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: On the 65 ter list, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Right. Have you submitted everything for translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe we have from the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Have you then identified among those documents the ones that don't actually need to be translated because there will be a few translated that are representative of the others?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think we have in certain instances where we've withdrawn exhibits, where we are no longer seeking those but I think for the bulk of those the issue of doing a selective sample is relating to particular exhibits not with respect to the 65 ter exhibits. It was with respect to the one exhibit that we had that was 700 and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And it was with respect to another exhibit which we did withdraw as Your Honour might recall that was the log-book, so that has been withdrawn completely from this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So where you've got crime scene reports extending to 2.096 pages you seriously want all of these translated?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I have to sit down and look at -- I haven't had a chance to look at the report that CLSS has generated on this, so I don't know what particular exhibits they're talking about but we're talking about talking about documents that might need to be brought in from the bar table that might lead to respect to witnesses from particular municipalities. So in that sense, Your Honour, you're catching me sort of off guard on this since I didn't have a chance to prepare in advance to this to see exactly what the issue is. But I have been working on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You may wish to consider the e-mail that was sent to you yesterday, yesterday evening, and tell us more tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'll be happy to do so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The other matter which also relates to your case is the expert report, Exhibit 6D668, where we asked you to file a revised complete version of the report and annexes rather than a very large number of corrigenda or additional bits that were to be placed into it. I think it was to correct a number of minor errors. Now, there's been no response to that request and it's not something we can particularly order at this stage, but it could have implications later when you come to introduce it into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour. I will have to check on that. I do recall we had submitted a form of a corrigendum and I thought that everything else was undertaken but I will have to check with our staff --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What we want to hear from you tomorrow is that a preparation of a revised version including all these corrections is in hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'll work on it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And hopefully an indication of when that will be available.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'll see what I can do on it, Your Honour, keeping in mind that we are in court until this afternoon as well, so I'll try to get ahold of the office during the pause to see what I can find out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We shall resume tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 5th day of December, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.
